heading: CJ 394 Criminele Process Stukken, 1768, ff. 518-519v.
text: CJ 394 Criminele Process Stukken, 1768, ff. 518-519v.
Huijden den 23e Maij 1768.

Compareerde voor mij Abraham Faure secretaris van Stellenbosch en Drakenstein, present de nagem. getuijgen, den slaaf Perfors van de Caab, van competenten ouderdom, toebehorende den oud heemraad Monsr. Martin Melk, den welken ter requisitie van den heer landdrost mr. Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, verklaard hoe waar is:
html: Compareerde voor mij Abraham Faure secretaris van Stellenbosch en Drakenstein, present de nagem. getuijgen, den slaaf Perfors van de Caab, van competenten ouderdom, toebehorende den oud heemraad Monsr. Martin Melk, den welken ter requisitie van den heer landdrost mr. Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, verklaard hoe waar is:

text: Dat nu ruim twee maanden geleden op zekere avond na gissing negen uuren, wanneer den compt. ter zijner lijfheers woonplaats Elsenburg gent., uit de combuijs naar het slavenhuijs ging, heeft gesien, dat den mede slaaf Frans van Madagascar met een stok onder den arm, voor het gem. slavenhuijs heen en weer wandelden, dat den compt., die reeds had gehoord dat den mede slaaf Willem denselfden dag hem Frans in ’t eijkenbosch dronken en slapende bevonden hebbende, daarover had geslagen, oversulx wel dagte dat hij Frans gem. Willem mogelijk weder zoude willen slaan, voorts aan den slaaf Achillis die hem uit het slavenhuijs tegemoet kwam, heeft gesegt, dat voorm. Willem moette waarschouwen, dat Frans voor de deur was en hem Willem zoude waarnemen te slaan, waarop gesz. Achillis zig naar de slavinnen kamer, alwaar zig gem. Willem ophield, begeven hebbende, is den compt. voorts in opgem. slavenhuijs gegaan, zonder dat van het voorgevallen tusschen meerm. Willem en Frans, verder iets heeft gesien.

Willem ophield, begeven hebbende, is den compt. voorts in opgem. slavenhuijs gegaan, zonder dat van het voorgevallen tusschen meerm. Willem en Frans, verder iets heeft gesien.

text: Anders niet verklarende geeft den compt. voor reedenen van wetenschap als in den text, bereijd zijnde, het voorenstaand des vereijscht werdende, nader te zullen gestand doen.
html: Anders niet verklarende geeft den compt. voor reedenen van wetenschap als in den text, bereijd zijnde, het voorenstaand des vereijscht werdende, nader te zullen gestand doen.

text: Dat aldus passeerde ter secretarije aan Stellenbosch, ter presentatie van den substitut, Johan Godlob John en den bode Johan Martin Smalberger, als getuijgen; die de minute deeses, benevens den compt. en mij secrets., mede behoorlijk hebben onderteekend.
html: Dat aldus passeerde ter secretarije aan Stellenbosch, ter presentatie van den substitut, Johan Godlob John en den bode Johan Martin Smalberger, als getuijgen; die de minute deeses, benevens den compt. en mij secrets., mede behoorlijk hebben onderteekend.

text: ’Twelk ik getuijge, [get.] A. Faure, secrets.
Recollement

Compareerde voor ons ondergete. gecommitteerdens uijt den E. Agtb. Raad van Justitie deeses gouvernements, voorm. Perfoos [sic] van de Caab, dewelke, deese sijne voorenstaande depositie van woorde tot woorde klaar en duijdelijk voorgeleesen zijnde, verklaarde daar bij ten vollen te persisteeren, niet begeerende, dat er iets meer bij gevoegt ofte van gedaan werden sal, als alleenig, dat hij compt. voorsz. Frans wel een half uur lang heeft sien wandelen voor ’t slavenhuijs, naast het welke de deur van de slavinnen kagie is, waarna gem. Frans beseijden de deur van het jongenshuijs [onleesbaar] gaan sitten, altoos soo wandelende als sittende naar ’t slavinnenhuijs gesien had, dog dat geene slavin, nog Silvia, Mars ofte eene andere, bij gem. Frans geweest of door hem compt. gesien was; als meede dat Frans ten die tijd nugterer was geweest en betuijgde in presentie van den slaaf Frans, alle ’t voorenstaande de waarheijd te sijn.

Frans wel een half uur lang heeft sien wandelen voor ’t slavenhuijs, naast het welke de deur van de slavinnen kagie is, waarna gem. Frans beseijden de deur van het jongenshuijs [onleesbaar] gaan sitten, altoos soo wandelende als sittende naar ’t slavinnenhuijs gesien had, dog dat geene slavin, nog Silvia, Mars ofte eene andere, bij gem. Frans geweest of door hem compt. gesien was; als meede dat Frans ten die tijd nugterer was geweest en betuijgde in presentie van den slaaf Frans, alle ’t voorenstaande de waarheijd te sijn.

text: Mij praesent, [get.] C.L. Neethling, secrets.
TRANSLATION

Today, 23 May 1768, there appears before me, Abraham Faure, secretary of Stellenbosch and Drakenstein, in the presence of the witnesses named below, the slave Perfors van de Caab, of competent age, belonging to the former heemraad, monsieur Martin Melk, who, on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, meester Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, declares it to be true:
html: Today, 23 May 1768, there appears before me, Abraham Faure, secretary of Stellenbosch and Drakenstein, in the presence of the witnesses named below, the slave Perfors van de Caab, of competent age, belonging to the former heemraad, monsieur Martin Melk, who, on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, meester Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, declares it to be true:

text: That fully two months ago now, on a certain evening at approximately 9 o’clock, when the testifier went from the kitchen to the slave house on his owner’s residential farm, called Elsenburg, he saw his fellow slave Frans van Madagascar walking up and down in front of the said slave house with a stick under his arm. That the testifier – who had already heard that his fellow slave Willem had that same day found Frans drunk and sleeping in the oak forest, and had beaten him over this – thought that Frans might possibly want to beat the said Willem because of this. He then told the slave Achilles, who was coming in his direction from the slave house, that he must warn the aforementioned Willem that Frans was in front of the door and might beat him when he sees him, upon which the said Achilles went to the women slaves’ room, which is where the said Willem lived, and the testifier went to the aforementioned slave house, without having seen anything further of what had happened between the said Willem and Frans.
html: That fully two months ago now, on a certain evening at approximately 9 o’clock, when the testifier went from the kitchen to the slave house on his owner’s residential farm, called Elsenburg, he saw his fellow slave Frans van Madagascar walking up and down in front of the said slave house with a stick under his arm. That the testifier – who had already heard that his fellow slave Willem had that same day found Frans drunk and sleeping in the oak forest, and had beaten him over this – thought that Frans might possibly want to beat the said Willem because of this. He then told the slave Achilles, who was coming in his direction from the slave house, that he must warn the aforementioned Willem that Frans was in front of the door and might beat him when he sees him, upon which the said Achilles went to the women slaves’ room, which is where the said Willem lived, and the testifier went to the aforementioned slave house, without having seen anything further of what had happened between the said Willem and Frans.

text: There being nothing else to declare, the testifier asserts to be convinced of the accuracy of his statement as in the text, being willing to subsequently confirm the above, if so required.
html: There being nothing else to declare, the testifier asserts to be convinced of the accuracy of his statement as in the text, being willing to subsequently confirm the above, if so required.

text: Thus recorded in the office of the secretary of Stellenbosch, in the presence of the deputy landdrost, Johan Godlob John, and the messenger of the court, Johan Martin Smalberger, as witnesses, who have properly signed the original of this, together with the testifier and me, the secretary.
html: Thus recorded in the office of the secretary of Stellenbosch, in the presence of the deputy landdrost, Johan Godlob John, and the messenger of the court, Johan Martin Smalberger, as witnesses, who have properly signed the original of this, together with the testifier and me, the secretary.

text: Which I declare, [signed] A. Faure, secretary.
Verification

There appears before us, the undersigned delegates from the honourable Council of Justice of this government, the aforementioned Perfors van de Caab, who, after this, his deposition above, was read out word by word, clearly and plainly, declares to fully persist by it, not desiring that anything more be added to or taken from it, except only that he, the testifier, in fact saw the aforesaid Frans walking for half an hour in front of the slave house, next to which is the door of the women slaves’ sleeping place, after which the said Frans went to sit beside the door of the jongens’ house, continually, both when walking and when sitting, staring at the women slaves’ house, yet that no woman slave, neither Silvia, Mars or any other, was with the said Frans, or was seen by the testifier, and also that Frans was more sober at this time; and declares in the presence of the slave Frans all of the aforegoing to be the truth.

heading: CJ 394 Criminele Process Stukken, 1768, ff. 520-522v.
text: CJ 394 Criminele Process Stukken, 1768, ff. 520-522v.

Relaas gegeven ter requisitie van den heer landdrost mr. Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, door den slaaf Achillis [sic] van Madagascar, van competenten ouderdom, toebehorende den oud heemraad monsr. Martin Melk, inhoudende als volgt:
html: Relaas gegeven ter requisitie van den heer landdrost mr. Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, door den slaaf Achillis [sic] van Madagascar, van competenten ouderdom, toebehorende den oud heemraad monsr. Martin Melk, inhoudende als volgt:

text: Dat eenigen tijd geleden die den relatant niet wel wist te bepalen, op zeekeren avond, wanneer denselven ter woonplaats van zijn lijfheer, uit het slavenhuijs kwam, door den slaaf Perfors ontmoet en gezegt geworden zijnde, dat hij relat. den slaaf Willem moette waarschouwen, dat den medeslaaf Frans daar buijten met een kirrij op hem paste, en hem Willem wilde slaan, den relatant zig voorts naar de meijdenkamer alwaar gem. Willem zijn slaapsstede had, begeven, en hem Willem sulx aangesegt hebbende, denselve daarop buijten de deur van dat vertrek is gekomen, en voorsz. Frans in deeser voegen heeft aangesproken: Frans wilt gij mijn slaan, waarop gem. Frans gevraagd hebbende Wie zegt dat? door gesz. Willem wierd geantwoord, Ik weet dat gij mijn slaan wilt. Op ’twelke meerm. Willem zig omkeerde alsof wederom in voorm. vertrek wilde gaan terwijl den relatant ondertusschen vandaar wat terugwaards geweken zijnde, op dat ogenblik heeft gezien, dat gerepten Frans een stok die hij in handen had, opgeligt en hem Willem daarmede een slag heeft gegeven, waarop denselven Willem plotslings ter aarde is komen neder te vallen, na ’twelke veelgem. Frans van daar weggelopen, en den relat. zig voorts naar ’t slavenhuijs gespoed hebbende, sulx de andere slaven heeft bekend gemaakt.

text: Aldus gerelateerd ter secretarije aan Stellenbosch, den 23 Maij 1768 ter presentie van den substitut Johan Godlob John en den bode Johan Martin Smalberger, als getuijgen, die de minute deeses benevens den compt. en mij secrets. mede behoorlijk hebben onderteekend.
html: Aldus gerelateerd ter secretarije aan Stellenbosch, den 23 Maij 1768 ter presentie van den substitut Johan Godlob John en den bode Johan Martin Smalberger, als getuijgen, die de minute deeses benevens den compt. en mij secrets. mede behoorlijk hebben onderteekend.

text: ’Twelk ik getuijge, [get.] A. Faure, secrets.
Recollement

Compareerde voor ons ondergete. gecommitteerdens uijt den E. Agtb. Raad van Justitie deeses gouvernements, voorm. Achillis van Madagascar, denwelken dit zijn gegeeven relaas van woorde tot woorde klaar en duijdelijk voorgeleesen sijnde verklaarde daarbij ten vollen te persisteeren, niet begeerende, dat er iets meer bij gevoegt ofte van gedaan werden sal, als allenig dat naar dat voorsz. Frans van sijn werk gekomen en een tijd lang in het slavenhuijs geweest was, denselven vervolgens door hem en Perfors <was gesient>  voor ’t  slavinnen huijs, heen en weer wandel en, sonder dat den compt. egter een kirrij in de handen, of onder ’t camisool van gem. Frans had gesien; dat voorsz. Frans aldaar eenigen tijd gewandelt hebbende, voorts op de aarde was gaan sitten tusschen de deuren van ’t jongens en meijdenhuijs; alwaar voorm. Willem, op der compt. waarschouwinge, buijten de meijdekamer gekomen sijnde, van denselven was gegaan en aan gem. Frans <,sonder hem door Willem een klap te hebben sien geeven,> de voorsz. vrage gedaan had. Betuijgende den compt. dat meerm. Frans, diens avond niet dronken, maar wel nugteren geweest was, en geduurende den tijd dat voor ’t meijdenhuijs heen en weeder gewandelt had, altoos naar de meijden kagie <had> gesien, eeven alsof iemand vanuijt hetselve afwagten, ’tgeen aan Perfors misschien had doen denken dat op Willem had gepast, seggende den compt. dat gem. Frans omtrent den tijd van een uur lang, invoegen voorsz. voor de meijden kamer gewandelt en tusschen de weederseijtsche deuren geseeten had, sonder dat de slavinnen Silvia en Mars aldaar bij hem geweest ofte neevens hem geseeten hadden; en betuijgde in presentie van den slaaf Frans alle ’t voorenstaande de waarheid te sijn.

text: Mij praesent, [get.] C.L. Neethling, secrets.
TRANSLATION

Statement given on the requisition of the honourable landdrost Meester Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, by the slave Achilles van Madagascar, of competent age, belonging to the former heemraad, Monsieur Martin Melk, of the following content:
html: Statement given on the requisition of the honourable landdrost Meester Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, by the slave Achilles van Madagascar, of competent age, belonging to the former heemraad, Monsieur Martin Melk, of the following content:

text: That on a certain evening some time ago, which the deponent cannot specify any closer, when he left the slave house on the residential farm of his owner, he was met by the slave Perfors and told that he must warn the slave Willem that his fellow slave Frans was waiting outside for him with a kirrij and wanted to beat him, Willem. The deponent then went to the meijden’s room, where the said Willem had his sleeping place, and told him this; upon which the same came out of that room and said something to the aforesaid Frans along these lines: “Frans, do you want to hit me?”, to which the said Frans replied: “Who says that?”, and was answered by Willem: “I know that you want to beat me”. Upon this the aforementioned Willem turned himself around as if wanting to go into the room again, at which moment the deponent, who in the meantime had been retreating a bit backwards from there, saw the said Frans lifting a stick which he held in his hands and giving Willem a blow with it, whereupon the same Willem suddenly fell down to the ground; after which the aforementioned Frans ran away from there, and the deponent rushed to the slave house where he made this known to the other slaves.
html: That on a certain evening some time ago, which the deponent cannot specify any closer, when he left the slave house on the residential farm of his owner, he was met by the slave Perfors and told that he must warn the slave Willem that his fellow slave Frans was waiting outside for him with a kirrij and wanted to beat him, Willem. The deponent then went to the meijden’s room, where the said Willem had his sleeping place, and told him this; upon which the same came out of that room and said something to the aforesaid Frans along these lines: “Frans, do you want to hit me?”, to which the said Frans replied: “Who says that?”, and was answered by Willem: “I know that you want to beat me”. Upon this the aforementioned Willem turned himself around as if wanting to go into the room again, at which moment the deponent, who in the meantime had been retreating a bit backwards from there, saw the said Frans lifting a stick which he held in his hands and giving Willem a blow with it, whereupon the same Willem suddenly fell down to the ground; after which the aforementioned Frans ran away from there, and the deponent rushed to the slave house where he made this known to the other slaves.

text: There being nothing further to declare, the deponent asserts to be convinced of the certainty of his statement as in the text, being willing to subsequently confirm the above, if so required.

text: Thus recorded at the office of the secretary of Stellenbosch, the 23rd of May 1768, in the presence of the deputy landdrost, Johan Godlob John, and the messenger of the court, Johan Martin Smalberger, as witnesses, who have properly signed the original of this, together with the testifier and me, the secretary.

text: Which I declare, [signed] A. Faure, secretary.
Verification

There appears before us, the undersigned delegates from the honourable Council of Justice of this government, the aforementioned Achilles van Madagascar, who, after this, his statement given, was read out word by word, clearly and plainly, declares to fully persist by it, not desiring that anything more be added to or taken from it, except only that after the aforesaid Frans had come from his work and had been in the slave house for a while, he was seen by him and Perfors walking up and down in front of the women slaves’ house, without, however, the testifier having seen a kirrij in the hands or under the camisole of the said Frans; that after the aforesaid Frans had been walking there for some time, he then went to sit down on the ground between the doors of the jongens’ and meijden’s houses; where the aforesaid Willem, on the testifier’s warning, came outside the room of the meijden and went from there to ask Frans the aforesaid question, without having seen him being given a slap by Willem. The testifier declares further that the aforementioned Frans was not drunk that evening, but in fact sober, and during the time that he had been walking up and down in front of the meijden’s house he was continually staring at the sleeping place of the meijden, just as if he was waiting for somebody from there, which made Perfors think that he was watching for Willem; the testifier adding that the said Frans was walking in front of the meijden’s room and sitting between the two doors for about an hour’s time, without the women slaves Silvia and Mars being there with him or sitting next to him, and declares in the presence of the slave Frans all of the above to be the truth.

heading: 1/STB 3/11 Criminele Verklaringen, 1759-1782, unpaginated.
text: 1/STB 3/11 Criminele Verklaringen, 1759-1782, unpaginated.

Relaas gegeven ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Mr. Jacobus Johannes Le Suëur door den slaaf Sijlvester van de Caab, van competenten ouderdom, toebehorende den burger Hendrik Louw, inhoudende als volgt:
html: Relaas gegeven ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Mr. Jacobus Johannes Le Suëur door den slaaf Sijlvester van de Caab, van competenten ouderdom, toebehorende den burger Hendrik Louw, inhoudende als volgt:

text: Dat nu omtrend twee weken geleden zonder dat den relatant den netten dag wist te bepalen, wanneer den medeslaaf Prins van Bengalen, die ter gem. zijnen lijfheers plaats gent. De Eijke Bomen, den wijngaard had opgepast, en door zijnen lijfheer belast was geworden, de varkens die daar in quamen ’er uit te slaan, gem. Prins eene dier dieren de lendenen ingeslagen en zig voorts ter vlugt heeft begeven.
html: Dat nu omtrend twee weken geleden zonder dat den relatant den netten dag wist te bepalen, wanneer den medeslaaf Prins van Bengalen, die ter gem. zijnen lijfheers plaats gent. De Eijke Bomen, den wijngaard had opgepast, en door zijnen lijfheer belast was geworden, de varkens die daar in quamen ’er uit te slaan, gem. Prins eene dier dieren de lendenen ingeslagen en zig voorts ter vlugt heeft begeven.

text: Dat denselven na eenige dagen zig daar omstreeks schuijl te hebben gehouden, op eenen Vrijdag namiddag door den schapenwagter in name Abraham, gevangen en thuijs gebragt zijnde, des relats. lijfheer ged. slaaf Prins voorts in de stal hebbende doen gaan, denselven door den relatant de beijde handen met een riem doen binden, en aan een balk aldaar heeft doen ophangen, als wanneer hun lijfheer gem. slaaf Prins de broek hebbende doen afnemen, met een sjambok zodanig over ’t lijf heeft geslagen dat ’er het bloed uitquam, gevende de sjambok wijders aan den relat. met ordre van in het slaan verder voor te varen, hetgeen door den relatant is gedaan geworden zo lange totdat belast wierd daarmede op te houden, en voorm. Prins los te maken, ’twelk dan ook door den relat. verrigt geworden weesende, is denselven Prins vervolgens van daar naar de dorschvloer gegaan, en aldaar tot des avonds bij ’t volk in ’t werk verbleven.  Dat des anderendaags morgens meergem. Prins door zijnen lijfheer belast geworden zijnde, de varkens van de dorschvloer naar het land te drijven, heeft denselven zig derwaards begeven, zonder wederom t’ huijs te zijn gekomen.

Prins los te maken, ’twelk dan ook door den relat. verrigt geworden weesende, is denselven Prins vervolgens van daar naar de dorschvloer gegaan, en aldaar tot des avonds bij ’t volk in ’t werk verbleven. Dat des anderendaags morgens meergem. Prins door zijnen lijfheer belast geworden zijnde, de varkens van de dorschvloer naar het land te drijven, heeft denselven zig derwaards begeven, zonder wederom t’ huijs te zijn gekomen.

text: Betuijgende den relatant al verder, dat zijn lijfheer hem heeft verboden, alhier te verklaren, dat voorsz. slaaf Prins gebonden en opgehangen is geweest.
html: Betuijgende den relatant al verder, dat zijn lijfheer hem heeft verboden, alhier te verklaren, dat voorsz. slaaf Prins gebonden en opgehangen is geweest.

Statement given on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, meester Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, by the slave Sijlvester van de Caab, of competent age, belonging to the burgher Hendrik Louw, of the following content:
html: Statement given on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, meester Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, by the slave Sijlvester van de Caab, of competent age, belonging to the burgher Hendrik Louw, of the following content:

text: That about two weeks ago now, without the deponent being able to ascertain the right day, when his fellow slave Prins van Bengalen, who was looking after the vineyard on his owner’s farm, named De Eijkebomen, was ordered by his owner to chase out the pigs who come in there, the said Prins smashed in the back of one of these animals and then set off in flight.
html: That about two weeks ago now, without the deponent being able to ascertain the right day, when his fellow slave Prins van Bengalen, who was looking after the vineyard on his owner’s farm, named De Eijkebomen, was ordered by his owner to chase out the pigs who come in there, the said Prins smashed in the back of one of these animals and then set off in flight.

text: That after hiding in that vicinity for some days, the same was taken prisoner and brought home late on a Friday afternoon by the shepherd named Abraham. The owner of the deponent then made the said slave Prins go into the stable, had both his hands tied up with a strap by the deponent, and had him hoisted up to a beam, which is when their owner had the trousers of the said slave Prins taken down and beat him with a sjambok over his body in such a manner that blood came from it, giving moreover the sjambok to the deponent with the command to continue further with the beating, which was done by the deponent until he was ordered to cease and to untie the aforementioned Prins, which was then done by the deponent, after which Prins went from there to the threshing-floor and remained there working with the other volk until the evening. That during the following morning, when the aforementioned Prins was ordered by his owner to drive the pigs from the threshing-floor to the field, the same set out thither, without returning home again.
html: That after hiding in that vicinity for some days, the same was taken prisoner and brought home late on a Friday afternoon by the shepherd named Abraham. The owner of the deponent then made the said slave Prins go into the stable, had both his hands tied up with a strap by the deponent, and had him hoisted up to a beam, which is when their owner had the trousers of the said slave Prins taken down and beat him with a sjambok over his body in such a manner that blood came from it, giving moreover the sjambok to the deponent with the command to continue further with the beating, which was done by the deponent until he was ordered to cease and to untie the aforementioned Prins, which was then done by the deponent, after which Prins went from there to the threshing-floor and remained there working with the other volk until the evening. That during the following morning, when the aforementioned Prins was ordered by his owner to drive the pigs from the threshing-floor to the field, the same set out thither, without returning home again.

text: The deponent also declares further that his owner had forbidden him to testify here that the aforesaid slave Prins had been tied and hung up.
html: The deponent also declares further that his owner had forbidden him to testify here that the aforesaid slave Prins had been tied and hung up.

text: There being nothing else to relate further, the deponent asserts to be convinced of the accuracy of his statement as in the text, being willing, if so required, to subsequently confirm the above.

Relaas gegeven ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Mr. Jacobus Johannes Le Suëur, door den burger Hendrik Louw van competenten ouderdom, zijnde van den volgende inhoud namentlijk:
html: Relaas gegeven ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Mr. Jacobus Johannes Le Suëur, door den burger Hendrik Louw van competenten ouderdom, zijnde van den volgende inhoud namentlijk:

text: Dat na des relatants gissing op den 9e der jongst gepasseerde maand Februarij wanneer denselven des morgens van den Caab thuijs was gekomen, desselfs slaaf Prins van Bengalen die den wijngaard heeft moeten oppassen, belast hebbende dat wel sorge moesten dragen wanneer de varkens aldaar kwamen deselve er uit te jagen, den relat. voorts zig ter rusten heeft begeven, wanneer tegens den middag opgestaan zijnde heeft gesien dat er eenig varkens in de wijngaard liepen, daarop een klijne jongen gent. Matthijs derwaards heeft gesonden om die dieren er uit te drijven, denwelke wederom terugge komende heeft gerapporteerd, dat voorm. Prins aldaar niet had vernomen. Dat den relat. wijders des namiddags omstreeks den wijngaard naar ged. slaaf hebbende doen soeken, zonder denselven te hebben opgespeurd, tegens den avond aldaar een varken dat de lendenen was ingeslagen, is gevonden geworden.
html: Dat na des relatants gissing op den 9e der jongst gepasseerde maand Februarij wanneer denselven des morgens van den Caab thuijs was gekomen, desselfs slaaf Prins van Bengalen die den wijngaard heeft moeten oppassen, belast hebbende dat wel sorge moesten dragen wanneer de varkens aldaar kwamen deselve er uit te jagen, den relat. voorts zig ter rusten heeft begeven, wanneer tegens den middag opgestaan zijnde heeft gesien dat er eenig varkens in de wijngaard liepen, daarop een klijne jongen gent. Matthijs derwaards heeft gesonden om die dieren er uit te drijven, denwelke wederom terugge komende heeft gerapporteerd, dat voorm. Prins aldaar niet had vernomen. Dat den relat. wijders des namiddags omstreeks den wijngaard naar ged. slaaf hebbende doen soeken, zonder denselven te hebben opgespeurd, tegens den avond aldaar een varken dat de lendenen was ingeslagen, is gevonden geworden.

text: Dat des Vrijdags den 12e daar aanvolgende, omtrend den middag voorm. slaaf Prins door des relats. schapenwagter in naame Abraham die denselven Prins in ’t veld omtrend de Berg Rivier bij den schapenwagter van den burgercornet David de Villiers J. Pz. gevangen genomen hebbende, is thuijs gebragt geworden; waarop den relat. voorts gem. jongen over zijn gedoente, principaal over het dikwils opdrossen, selfs hebbende willen straffen, om reedenen wijl hij relat. des volgende daags ter verrigting zijner affairs, zig weder Caabwaards moeste begeven, en gem.  Prins door een andere slaaf, uit hoofde deeser droevige tijdsomstandigheid, niet wel naar Stellenbosch ter afstraffing durfde zenden, gelijk ook uit vreese van door een lopende loesing of kastijding, aan ged. slaaf onder ’t worsteling mogelijk eenen ongelukkigen slag mogte werden toegebragt, dierhalven de beijde handen door de slaaf Sijlvester met een riem aan elkanderen hebbende doen binden, voorts in de stal gebragt, en aldaar, na hem alvorens de broek te hebben doen afstrijken, werdende denselven ondertusschen door voorm. Sijlvester vast gehouden, eenige slagen met een sjambok over de billen heeft gegeven, vervolgens de riem over een balk geworpen en hem Prins aan een bij de kribben staande paal hebbende doen vast binden, den relat. de sjambok aan ged. slaaf Sijlvester wijders heeft overgegeven, met last van meerm. Prins daar mede te slaan, hetgeen gesz.  Sijlvester dan ook ter presentie van den relatant heeft verrigt, dog den relat. onder ’t slaan bemerkende dat veelgem. Prins eenige slagen over de rug en lendenen wierden toegebragt, heeft sulx gesz. Sijlvester verboden en gesegt alleenlijk over de billen te slaan; waarna den relat. vermeenende meerm. slaaf Prins genoeg te hebben doen kastijden, denselven wederom heeft doen losmaken en voorts naar de dorschvloer gesonden, alwaar hij Prins tot des avonds bij ’t volk in ’t werk is verbleven, en met deselve in ’t huijs gekomen wesende zijl. tesamen het avondstuk hebben gegeten.

Sijlvester vast gehouden, eenige slagen met een sjambok over de billen heeft gegeven, vervolgens de riem over een balk geworpen en hem Prins aan een bij de kribben staande paal hebbende doen vast binden, den relat. de sjambok aan ged. slaaf Sijlvester wijders heeft overgegeven, met last van meerm. Prins daar mede te slaan, hetgeen gesz. Sijlvester dan ook ter presentie van den relatant heeft verrigt, dog den relat. onder ’t slaan bemerkende dat veelgem. Prins eenige slagen over de rug en lendenen wierden toegebragt, heeft sulx gesz. Sijlvester verboden en gesegt alleenlijk over de billen te slaan; waarna den relat. vermeenende meerm. slaaf Prins genoeg te hebben doen kastijden, denselven wederom heeft doen losmaken en voorts naar de dorschvloer gesonden, alwaar hij Prins tot des avonds bij ’t volk in ’t werk is verbleven, en met deselve in ’t huijs gekomen wesende zijl. tesamen het avondstuk hebben gegeten.

text: Dat des anderendaags ’s morgens den relat. op den dorschvloer gekomen zijnde, en voorsz.  Prins bij ’t volk aldaar niet vernomen, maar verstaan hebbende dat zig nog in ’t slavenhuijs bevond, hem Prins heeft doen roepen en bevolen om bij ’t volk op den vloer te werken, zijnde den relatant voorts weder naar het huijs gegaan, als wanneer de relat.  dien eigen morgen wederom bij den dorschvloer komende en veelgem. Prins aldaar vermissende op gedaane afvrage kwam te vernemen, dat hij door het volk was belast geworden om de varkens van daar naar de rivier te drijven, en dus die dag niet weder te voorschijn gekomen wesende, de relat. denselven te vergeefs heeft doen opsoeken.

Prins bij ’t volk aldaar niet vernomen, maar verstaan hebbende dat zig nog in ’t slavenhuijs bevond, hem Prins heeft doen roepen en bevolen om bij ’t volk op den vloer te werken, zijnde den relatant voorts weder naar het huijs gegaan, als wanneer de relat. dien eigen morgen wederom bij den dorschvloer komende en veelgem. Prins aldaar vermissende op gedaane afvrage kwam te vernemen, dat hij door het volk was belast geworden om de varkens van daar naar de rivier te drijven, en dus die dag niet weder te voorschijn gekomen wesende, de relat. denselven te vergeefs heeft doen opsoeken.

text: Anders niet relateerende geeft de relat. voor reedenen van wetenschap als in de text, bereijd zijnde, het vorenstaande des gerequireerd werdende, met solemnelen eede nader te zullen gestand doen.

text: TRANSLATION
Statement given on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, meester Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, by the burgher Hendrik Louw, of competent age, being of the following content, namely:
html: Statement given on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, meester Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, by the burgher Hendrik Louw, of competent age, being of the following content, namely:

text: That, by his estimate, on the 9th of the just passed month February when the deponent came home from the Cape during the morning, he instructed his slave Prins van Bengalen, who had to look after the vineyard, to make sure, when the pigs come in there, that they are chased away. The deponent then went to rest and when he got up in the afternoon, he saw that there were some pigs walking in the vineyard, whereupon he sent a small jongen called Matthijs to drive the animals out of there, who, when he came back again, reported that he had not seen the aforementioned Prins there. That late in the afternoon the deponent again had people looking for the said slave in the vicinity of the vineyard, without finding him, but that by evening a pig whose back was smashed in was found there.
html: That, by his estimate, on the 9th of the just passed month February when the deponent came home from the Cape during the morning, he instructed his slave Prins van Bengalen, who had to look after the vineyard, to make sure, when the pigs come in there, that they are chased away. The deponent then went to rest and when he got up in the afternoon, he saw that there were some pigs walking in the vineyard, whereupon he sent a small jongen called Matthijs to drive the animals out of there, who, when he came back again, reported that he had not seen the aforementioned Prins there. That late in the afternoon the deponent again had people looking for the said slave in the vicinity of the vineyard, without finding him, but that by evening a pig whose back was smashed in was found there.

text: That at about noon on Friday the 12th, the aforementioned slave Prins was brought home by the shepherd of the deponent, called Abraham, who had taken the same Prins prisoner in the veld around the Bergriver at the shepherd of the burgher cornet David de Villiers J. Pz.; whereupon the deponent himself wanted to punish the aforementioned jongen for his deeds, principally over his frequent running away, because, as the deponent again had to set out the following day to the Cape on business, and therefore did not dare, considering this unfortunate time constraint, to have the said Prins taken by another slave to Stellenbosch for punishment. Similarly, fearing also that with the ongoing hiding or punishment the said slave might be given an unfortunate blow during the struggle, he therefore had both his hands tied to each other with a strap by the slave Sijlvester, then brought him into the stable, and there, after first having had his trousers taken down, and while he was in the meantime being held tight by the aforementioned Sijlvester, he gave him some strokes with the sjambok on his buttocks. Afterwards the deponent threw the strap over the beam and had him, Prins, tied to a pole, which stood by the mangers, and handed over the sjambok to the said slave Sijlvester, with the command to beat the aforementioned Prins with it, which Sijlvester then did in the presence of the deponent. However, when the deponent noticed during the beating that the said Prins was being given some strokes on his back and legs, he forbade Sijlvester this and told him to only beat him on the buttocks. When the deponent was of the opinion that the aforementioned slave Prins had been punished sufficiently, he had him untied again and sent him to the threshing-floor, where he, Prins, remained working with the volk until the evening and, having come home with the same, they together ate their evening meal.
html: That at about noon on Friday the 12th, the aforementioned slave Prins was brought home by the shepherd of the deponent, called Abraham, who had taken the same Prins prisoner in the veld around the Bergriver at the shepherd of the burgher cornet David de Villiers J. Pz.; whereupon the deponent himself wanted to punish the aforementioned jongen for his deeds, principally over his frequent running away, because, as the deponent again had to set out the following day to the Cape on business, and therefore did not dare, considering this unfortunate time constraint, to have the said Prins taken by another slave to Stellenbosch for punishment. Similarly, fearing also that with the ongoing hiding or punishment the said slave might be given an unfortunate blow during the struggle, he therefore had both his hands tied to each other with a strap by the slave Sijlvester, then brought him into the stable, and there, after first having had his trousers taken down, and while he was in the meantime being held tight by the aforementioned Sijlvester, he gave him some strokes with the sjambok on his buttocks. Afterwards the deponent threw the strap over the beam and had him, Prins, tied to a pole, which stood by the mangers, and handed over the sjambok to the said slave Sijlvester, with the command to beat the aforementioned Prins with it, which Sijlvester then did in the presence of the deponent. However, when the deponent noticed during the beating that the said Prins was being given some strokes on his back and legs, he forbade Sijlvester this and told him to only beat him on the buttocks. When the deponent was of the opinion that the aforementioned slave Prins had been punished sufficiently, he had him untied again and sent him to the threshing-floor, where he, Prins, remained working with the volk until the evening and, having come home with the same, they together ate their evening meal.

text: That in the morning of the following day, when the deponent went to the threshing-floor and did not see the aforesaid Prins with the volk there, but understood that he was still in the slave house, he had him called and ordered to come and work with the volk on the floor. The deponent then again went to the house but that same morning, when the deponent again went to the threshing-floor and found the aforementioned Prins missing from there, he learned in answer to his questions that he had been ordered by the volk to drive the pigs from there to the river, and did not reappear again that day. The deponent had searched for the same in vain.

The deponent then again went to the house but that same morning, when the deponent again went to the threshing-floor and found the aforementioned Prins missing from there, he learned in answer to his questions that he had been ordered by the volk to drive the pigs from there to the river, and did not reappear again that day. The deponent had searched for the same in vain.

text: There being nothing else to relate, the deponent asserts to be convinced of the accuracy of his statement as in the text, being willing, if so required, to subsequently confirm the above with solemn oaths.

text: 1/STB 3/11 Criminele Verklaringen, 1759-1782, unpaginated.

Relaas gegeven ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Mr. Jacobus Johannes Le Suëur, door den slaaf Prins van Bengalen van competenten ouderdom, toebehorende den burger Hendrik Louw, inhoudende als volgt:
html: Relaas gegeven ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Mr. Jacobus Johannes Le Suëur, door den slaaf Prins van Bengalen van competenten ouderdom, toebehorende den burger Hendrik Louw, inhoudende als volgt:

text: Dat nu ruim vijf weken geleden, wanneer den relatant ter zijner lijfheers plaats den wijngaard hebbende moeten oppassen, en de varkens die aldaar gedurig in deselve kwamen te lopen (als zijnde alleenlijk maar met eenige losse boschjes wat afgeschut) daar van niet wel hebbende kunnen afhouden, desselfs lijfheer op zeekeren dag terwijl denselven in den wijngaard komende en gesien hebbende dat er schade aan de stokken en druijven was geschied, hem relat., deswegens heeft bekeven en teffens belast, dat wanneer de varkens er weder in kwamen, den relat. als dan met een stok op deselve moeste raken en met slagen van daar verdrijven. Dat den relat. terwijl desselfs lijfheer intusschen naar de Caab gereden en nog afweesig was, door de slavinne Juliana gewaarschouwt zijnde dat ’er varkens in den wijngaard liepen, zig voorts derwaards heeft gespoed nemende een stok in de handen, waar mede hij relat. onder het uitdrijven dier dieren, eene derselve zodanig heeft geraakt dat deselve uit den wijngaard geraakt, kruipel lopende daaromtrend is blijven liggen, ’twelk den relatant dan ook aan het volk ter gem. plaats bescheijden, terstond heeft bekend gemaakt.
html: Dat nu ruim vijf weken geleden, wanneer den relatant ter zijner lijfheers plaats den wijngaard hebbende moeten oppassen, en de varkens die aldaar gedurig in deselve kwamen te lopen (als zijnde alleenlijk maar met eenige losse boschjes wat afgeschut) daar van niet wel hebbende kunnen afhouden, desselfs lijfheer op zeekeren dag terwijl denselven in den wijngaard komende en gesien hebbende dat er schade aan de stokken en druijven was geschied, hem relat., deswegens heeft bekeven en teffens belast, dat wanneer de varkens er weder in kwamen, den relat. als dan met een stok op deselve moeste raken en met slagen van daar verdrijven. Dat den relat. terwijl desselfs lijfheer intusschen naar de Caab gereden en nog afweesig was, door de slavinne Juliana gewaarschouwt zijnde dat ’er varkens in den wijngaard liepen, zig voorts derwaards heeft gespoed nemende een stok in de handen, waar mede hij relat. onder het uitdrijven dier dieren, eene derselve zodanig heeft geraakt dat deselve uit den wijngaard geraakt, kruipel lopende daaromtrend is blijven liggen, ’twelk den relatant dan ook aan het volk ter gem. plaats bescheijden, terstond heeft bekend gemaakt.

text: Dat des relats. lijfheer ’s daags daaraanvolgende thuijs gekomen, en van dit geval door de andere slaven berigt geworden zijnde, hem relat. daarover heeft willen slaan, waarop den relat. de vlugt genomen en zig daaromstreeks langs de Bergrivier heeft schuijl gehouden totdat den vierden dag daaraanvolgende den relat. zig bij een schapenwagter van David de Villiers J. Pz. vervoegd en aan denselven had voorgegeven dat hij naar een verloren paard sogte, door den anderen onderwijlen aan de praat wierd gehouden terwijl den mede slaaf Abraham met zijn lijfheers schapentroup aldaar in ’t veld wesende, hem relat. gevangen genomen, en voorts heeft thuijs gebragt.
html: Dat des relats. lijfheer ’s daags daaraanvolgende thuijs gekomen, en van dit geval door de andere slaven berigt geworden zijnde, hem relat. daarover heeft willen slaan, waarop den relat. de vlugt genomen en zig daaromstreeks langs de Bergrivier heeft schuijl gehouden totdat den vierden dag daaraanvolgende den relat. zig bij een schapenwagter van David de Villiers J. Pz. vervoegd en aan denselven had voorgegeven dat hij naar een verloren paard sogte, door den anderen onderwijlen aan de praat wierd gehouden terwijl den mede slaaf Abraham met zijn lijfheers schapentroup aldaar in ’t veld wesende, hem relat. gevangen genomen, en voorts heeft thuijs gebragt.

text: Dat des relats. lijfheer voorts onder bedreiging van hem naar Stellenbosch ter afstraffing te zenden, hem relat. door den slaaf Sijlvester de beijde handen met een riem hebbende doen vastbinden, in de stal aan een balk met de voeten van den grond, doen ophangen en terwijl gedagte Sijlvester den riem vast hield, nadat hem relat. de broek was afgestreken, met een sjambok over het bloote lijf geslagen, zijnde ondertusschen des relats. lijfvrouw aldaar gekomen dewelke versogte dat zijne lijfheer met het slaan moeste ophouden, waarop zijn lijfheer geantwoord hebbende hij heeft nog niet genoeg, de sjambok wijders aan gem. Sijlvester hebbende overgegeven, heeft belast met het slaan voort te varen, onder het seggen: Daar haald hem maar deur, hetgeen is verrigt geworden, niet tegenstaande des relats. lijfvrouw verscheijde malen had gesegt: Basta, ’t is al genoeg geslagen, zonder dat zijn lijfheer daar na wilde horen.  Dat den relat. vervolgens los gemaakte zijnde, door zijne lijfheer naar de dorschvloer is gesonden om met het volk aldaar te werken, zijnde kort daarop desselfs lijfheer mede aldaar gekomen, denwelken den relat. gevraagt hebbende, waar hij geduurende het drossen de kost gekregen, en een rok die den relat. van eene der andere slaven had medegenomen, heeft gelaten?; op ’twelke de relat. geantwoord hebbende zoals ’t geschied was, hem relat. door de mede slaven Jephta, Julij, Achillis en Augustus, op den vloer heeft nederleggen en vast houden, en voorts met de steel van een stroo vork verscheijde slagen op de billen heeft gegeven waarna desselfs lijfheer meerm. Sijlvester heeft belast te paard te stijgen en den relat. voor hetselven te doen lopen, ten einde voorsz. rok te gaan opsoeken dat den relat. nevens Sijlvester dien rok thuijs gebragt hebbende, andermaal ter ordre van zijnen lijfheer, door voorm. vier slaven invoegen als voren op den vloer nedergelegt en vastgehouden  wesende door gem. zijnen lijfheer wederom met een sjambok veele slagen over den rug zijn gegeven geworden.

text: Dat de relat. des anderdaags ’s morgens wegens gevoeligde pijn der ontfangene slagen in zijn kooij zijnde blijven liggen uit naam is geroepen en bevolen geworden naar het werk te gaan, en bij het volk op de dorschvloer gekomen weesende, vervolgens door veelgem. text: TRANSLATION

Statement given on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, meester Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, by the slave Prins van Bengalen, of competent age, belonging to the burgher Hendrik Louw, of the following content:
html: Statement given on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, meester Jacobus Johannes le Suëur, by the slave Prins van Bengalen, of competent age, belonging to the burgher Hendrik Louw, of the following content:

text: That fully five weeks ago now, when the deponent had to look after the vineyard on his owner’s farm and could not keep the pigs, who are forever coming to run around there (since it is only fenced off with some loose shrub), very well out of there, his owner, on a certain day when he came into the vineyard and noticed that damage had been done to the vines and grapes, rebuked him over this and at the same time ordered him that when the pigs come in there again, the deponent must hit them with a stick and must drive them from there with blows. That the deponent, while his owner meanwhile had ridden off to the Cape and was still absent, was warned by the woman slave Juliana that there were pigs running around in the vineyard, whereupon he sped thither, taking a stick in his hands with which he, while driving out these animals, hit one of them in such a way that it got out of the vineyard walking with a limp and then remained lying there, which the deponent then also at once made known to the volk working on the said farm.

text: That the owner of the deponent came home the following day and when he was informed of this incident by the other slaves, wanted to beat the deponent over it; whereupon the deponent took flight and kept himself hidden in the area along the Bergriver until the fourth day thereafter, when the deponent went to the shepherd of David de Villiers, J. Pz., and pretended to the same that he was looking for a lost horse, and while he was being kept occupied talking to him, he was taken prisoner by his fellow slave Abraham, who was there in the veld with his owner’s flock of sheep, and then brought home.

Pz., and pretended to the same that he was looking for a lost horse, and while he was being kept occupied talking to him, he was taken prisoner by his fellow slave Abraham, who was there in the veld with his owner’s flock of sheep, and then brought home.

text: That the deponent’ owner then, while threatening to send him to Stellenbosch for punishment, had his hands tied together by the slave Sijlvester with a strap, had him hung up in the stable to a beam with his feet above the ground and, while the said Sijlvester was holding the strap, and after his trousers were taken down, beat him with a sjambok on his naked body. In the meantime the deponent’s mistress came there and requested his owner to cease the beating, whereupon his owner answered: “He has not had enough yet”, and then handed the sjambok over to the said Sijlvester and ordered him to continue, saying: “There you go, thrash him thoroughly”, notwithstanding the deponent’s mistress saying several times: “Stop it, that is enough of a beating”, without his owner wanting to listen to this. That afterwards the deponent was untied, sent by his owner to the threshing-floor to work with the volk there, while his owner shortly thereafter also came there and asked the deponent where he got food during his desertion, and where he had left the coat of one of the other slaves which the deponent had taken with him, to which the deponent answered as it had happened; he was laid down on the floor and held tight by his fellow slaves Jephta, Julij, Achillis and Augustus, and then given several blows with the handle of a pitchfork on his buttocks, after which his owner ordered the aforementioned Sijlvester to mount a horse and to make the deponent run in front of it in order to go and search for the aforesaid coat; that the deponent, together with Sijlvester, brought this coat home, when he was once again, on the order of his owner, laid down on the floor and held tight by the aforementioned four slaves, just as before, and again given many strokes with a sjambok on his back.

text: That in the morning of the following day, because of the pain he was experiencing from the beatings he had received, the deponent remained in his bed, when he was called by name and ordered to go to work, and when he arrived at the volk on the threshing-floor, he was ordered by the aforementioned Sijlvester to drive the pigs from there to the river, which he did, and then betook himself to Stellenbosch to complain about his owner.

heading: 1774 to 1865 — The Gentle Paternalist (Petrus Borchardus Borcherds)
text: 1774 to 1865 — The Gentle Paternalist (Petrus Borchardus Borcherds)
html: 1774 to 1865 — The Gentle Paternalist (Petrus Borchardus Borcherds)

text: Editor’s Introduction

What is unusual about the following extract is that the author clearly shows how it was possible for a slave owner to believe that the slave society in which he lived was “mild” and in the same extract to describe a slave revolt which surely proved that the system was certainly not perceived by slaves as “mild.” This contradiction is not noted by the author, whom we must assume was insensitive to the true perceptions of the slaves even though he claimed to disapprove the institution. Like Samuel Eusebius Hudson (q.v.), Borcherds was one of the few colonists to write about his life and times. Moreover, both Hudson and Borcherds used the same metaphor—the family—to describe how the Cape slave society worked. It appears significant that two authors from quite dissimilar cultural backgrounds, English and Dutch, should describe the society in the same way. He was the eldest of ten children and himself fathered seventeen children, five of whom died young. Born in the Dutch period, he went on to serve the successive regimes--British (1795-1803), Batavian (1803-1806), and again British with equal zeal and loyalty.

text: Extract from An Autobiographical Memoir

No respectable family was seen without the Bible in its possession, some too with books of prayer or hymns, which, with other religious books, were read with attention and reverence. Some families owned a Flavius Josephus and books of martyrology, and it was not unusual to hear in some houses the singing of psalms and hymns before daylight and in the evening before supper; at meals, prayer and thanksgiving, either by the father, mother, one of the children, or schoolmaster, was observed, and in some families I cannot recollect to have seen it ever neglected; I know, when yet young, that religious instruction was given in the evening even to the slaves belonging to the household, particularly by a Mr. Frans Roos of Moddergat, Hamman of Stellenbosch, Roux, and others.

text: With regard to the slaves, notwithstanding the great power allowed to the masters, I think that in this country slavery existed in its mildest form; there was a good deal of kind feeling shown towards those slaves who had been inherited and those born in the family (huysboorlingen). I have seen several of the latter nursed by the mistress of the house, and treated precisely like her own children. In fact, they had become almost members of the family.

text: From the different modes of education, and through example, caprice, passion, exaction, and disposition of the different masters, there were undoubtedly exceptions; but coercion was at times required to check idleness and disobedience, especially in the instance of those imported Negroes, from whom it was natural to expect aversion to labour. It is true that in some instances the power granted by law to the masters was abused; but as this operated against the master's own interest, and was moreover checked by provisions of the law, which authorized the sale of an ill-treated slave, who could not be again purchased by his master's relations, and in some aggravated cases of all the slaves, and was moreover visited by additional fines or imprisonment, and in cases of murder, even with capital punishment,—cases of excessive ill-treatment I consider to have been rare compared to the others I have mentioned.

It is true that in some instances the power granted by law to the masters was abused; but as this operated against the master's own interest, and was moreover checked by provisions of the law, which authorized the sale of an ill-treated slave, who could not be again purchased by his master's relations, and in some aggravated cases of all the slaves, and was moreover visited by additional fines or imprisonment, and in cases of murder, even with capital punishment,—cases of excessive ill-treatment I consider to have been rare compared to the others I have mentioned.

text: Yet, in however mild a state slavery may be considered to have existed in the colony, the absolute power exercised by one human being over the other, the temptation and opportunity for doing so, and abusing it in the more distant localities without fear of detection or control, the separation of families by sale or other means, the scanty supply of food and clothing, the confined apartments allotted the slave, and several other circumstances, especially the immoral state of concubinage, all made it ever appear to my mind as a state in our society undesirable and contrary to the principles of Christianity and good morals, and unnatural between man and man, however much tolerated by custom and even protected by law.

text: Whether it was from principles imbibed from my father, who, born in East Friso, a country perfectly free, highly extolled the liberty of the subject and the non-existence of slavery in Europe, and the blessing of being served by free people and not serfs, or whether it was natural to my own feelings, I cannot say,—but there was something so repulsive in that state of bondage and so contrary to the principles of justice that when the day arrived of the slave emancipation in this colony, though I was a sufferer in a pecuniary point of view, I felt the event was a great blessing and benefit to the community at large, and was a tribute of infinite value to humanity.

text: Had the Home Government been fully acquainted with all local circumstances, and the actual inclination of the inhabitants to co-operate and promote emancipation, the manumission of the coloured races might have been effected in this colony at less expense and with more satisfaction to all parties.

text: At the period of which I now make mention there existed a Philanthropic Society for purchasing young female children, with the object of freeing them and leaving them with their parents or judiciously apprenticing them during their nonage. Had the funds  of that society been larger, it alone in a few years might have extinguished slavery; an annual grant of five thousand pounds, in addition to the subscriptions, would have been ample to effect gradually the object in view, and the result of such a measure less embarrassing to the owners, who were, strictly speaking, under the registry by Government established and countenanced in that species of property; and such was then the disposition to promote emancipation, that when a slave was offered at public sale, and it became known that he was to be purchased for freedom, custom and feeling forbade competition, so that he might be liberated for a moderate sum.

text: But I feel that the case of this colony could not have been made an isolated one; it stood closely connected with those of her sister colonies: the grand measure had been determined upon and adopted by the Imperial Parliament, that in the British dominions slavery should not exist, and the measure of compensation under valuation was resorted to.
html: But I feel that the case of this colony could not have been made an isolated one; it stood closely connected with those of her sister colonies: the grand measure had been determined upon and adopted by the Imperial Parliament, that in the British dominions slavery should not exist, and the measure of compensation under valuation was resorted to.

text: Had the payment been made in the colony, either through the treasury or commissariat, according to the valuation of the Government appraisers, the owners, especially landholders, would not have suffered to the extent some of them have, notwithstanding the distress through want of labour which was immediately felt. But the payment of the compensation was to be made in England; the appointment of agents to receive the money became consequently unavoidable, and this led to speculation and jobbery, to the profit of a few speculators but to the loss of the slave-holder. Reports were industriously spread wide and far of the uncertainty of payment, or rather the certainty of non-payment, of the compensation claims, which induced many ignorant of the true state of the matter to dispose of their claims at very reduced discount to the speculator who had perhaps helped to spread the report. Some who had bought their slaves on credit were pressed by their creditors for payment; others required capital to proceed with the culti¬vation of their lands by free labour and for other incidental expenses. I am under the impression that vast sums have been realized by some of the speculators, while great losses were sustained by those whom Government was desirous to compensate; and I have no doubt a discontent was thus created which ultimately led in the distant country districts to the emigration which soon after began to pour over the boundaries of the colony.

text: With regard to the slaves, it was but natural that their expression of joy should be great; and on the 1st of December, 1839, numbers were seen in groups with happy countenances proceeding to Cape Town. Some expected to find a large table with eatables spread on the Grand Parade, but they were of course disappointed. Much of their joyful expectations was damped by the day being an uncommonly rainy one, torrents of rain came down from the clouds. This caused the speedy retirement of many, and some returned to their old masters' homes and continued in their former service, and up to this date there are instances in which the former slaves reside and work for wages on the estates of their late owners; but many of them have gradually established themselves independent of service, and there is no doubt that the condition of that class has now been materially improved; they receive handsome wages when employed; and in the vicinity of Cape Town the weekly pleasure parties taking their excursions and picnics, and conveyed in wagons or other vehicles to the pleasant environs of Wynberg and Constantia, prove their comfortable state and position. Some have attached themselves to Christian churches and institutions, but most, especially in Cape Town, to the Mohammedans, with whom they were previously more or less connected.

Some expected to find a large table with eatables spread on the Grand Parade, but they were of course disappointed. Much of their joyful expectations was damped by the day being an uncommonly rainy one, torrents of rain came down from the clouds. This caused the speedy retirement of many, and some returned to their old masters' homes and continued in their former service, and up to this date there are instances in which the former slaves reside and work for wages on the estates of their late owners; but many of them have gradually established themselves independent of service, and there is no doubt that the condition of that class has now been materially improved; they receive handsome wages when employed; and in the vicinity of Cape Town the weekly pleasure parties taking their excursions and picnics, and conveyed in wagons or other vehicles to the pleasant environs of Wynberg and Constantia, prove their comfortable state and position. Some have attached themselves to Christian churches and institutions, but most, especially in Cape Town, to the Mohammedans, with whom they were previously more or less connected.

text: Charles Bell

When I consider the emancipation in point of humanity, my mind is imperceptibly drawn to that period before 1813, when the length of confinement in prison or degree of corporal punishment were in cases of domestic offences unlimited, and left in the hands of masters and at the discretion of the authorities. However, by Governor Sir John Francis Cradock, the corporal punishment in such cases was limited to thirty-nine lashes, and the public authorities having superintendence of any place of confinement were directed not to permit any slave to be detained for more than one month. That under the former system abuses of unlimited authority had been committed cannot be doubted; it is but the natural consequence of an uncontrolled arbitrary power left in the hands of human beings guided by self-interest.

However, by Governor Sir John Francis Cradock, the corporal punishment in such cases was limited to thirty-nine lashes, and the public authorities having superintendence of any place of confinement were directed not to permit any slave to be detained for more than one month. That under the former system abuses of unlimited authority had been committed cannot be doubted; it is but the natural consequence of an uncontrolled arbitrary power left in the hands of human beings guided by self-interest.

text: As deputy fiscal in Cape Town it was part of my duty to dispose of cases between masters and slaves. The limitation made as to the degree of punishment was to my mind very relieving. Constant, I may say almost daily, applications were made to have slaves punished at the prison, under statements and accusations of various domestic offences. And though I feel at this moment some satisfaction at having in several instances succeeded in obtaining pardon, in others a restraint in the exercise of that authority which was licensed by the law for the sake of keeping in a state of subjection and subordination that unfortunate class which was doomed by slavery to submit to the will of those who possessed them in bondage and who were deprived of the privileges of free subjects, yet I have my doubts whether in that difficult position several of these cases could be strictly tested by those rules for the administration of justice which at present favour the public trial of all offences. The state of compulsion and bondage created naturally in the slave the inclination to resist in bad temper even the lawful commands of the disposers of his servitude.

The state of compulsion and bondage created naturally in the slave the inclination to resist in bad temper even the lawful commands of the disposers of his servitude.

text: Comparing the number of punishments inflicted in those days with those since the emancipation, and especially in latter years when I held the magistracy of Cape Town, and when corporal punishment was rarely found necessary except for public crimes, I cannot but rejoice at the sparing of pain and human suffering in our society under the present state, now that slavery is unknown; and watching for some time back the state of crime, I am fully convinced that under the frequent infliction of corporal punishment, crime will not decrease, but harden and debase the human mind; whilst if but sparingly and suitably applied in cases where the law and circumstances will justify such severe exercise of power, the feelings of rectitude and correctness of conduct, and the interest in character, reputation, and self-respect is better preserved, and the body of the community at large kept in a more wholesome state in regard to crimes and offences.

text: I would state more on this important subject, were it not that I feel already to have extended the limits of this memoir, but the reader will, I trust, indulge me in a matter in which, both as a public man and a private citizen I have been deeply concerned.

text: It would require a separate volume to note the various cases decided and disposed of by the court of justice during my employment in their office, and would form an interesting collection of causes celebres. One, however, of the most remarkable in the days of slavery (and in which the emancipation from slavery has prevented from ever happening again) was about the expiration of the year 1808. It was that of an insurrection. I will endeavour to give a brief account, taken from the sentence. Such documents contained also, besides the judgment, the species facti of the crimes.

text: [The 1808 Slave Revolt ]

Some time previous to the month of October, 1808, it so happened that a certain James Hooper, an Irishman, lived in Cape Town with Louis, slave of a Mrs. Kirsten.  Hooper told him “that there were no slaves in his country and that every person was free.” And they concerted with another slave, Abraham, a plan to endeavour to make the slaves in this colony also free, and if need be to employ violent means. Louis undertook to speak to such slaves as he knew in the country; and he did so, first to some of a Mr. Louw, in Zwartland (now Malmesbury), and found them ready to assist.
html: Some time previous to the month of October, 1808, it so happened that a certain James Hooper, an Irishman, lived in Cape Town with Louis, slave of a Mrs. Kirsten. Hooper told him “that there were no slaves in his country and that every person was free.” And they concerted with another slave, Abraham, a plan to endeavour to make the slaves in this colony also free, and if need be to employ violent means. Louis undertook to speak to such slaves as he knew in the country; and he did so, first to some of a Mr. Louw, in Zwartland (now Malmesbury), and found them ready to assist.

text: Thus prepared, Hooper and Abraham proceeded to Louw's and spent the evening with him, Hooper pretending to be a gentleman and Abraham figuring as his servant.
html: Thus prepared, Hooper and Abraham proceeded to Louw's and spent the evening with him, Hooper pretending to be a gentleman and Abraham figuring as his servant.

text: The plan being communicated to one Michael Kelly, also an Irishman, he agreed to join, and Hooper hired a wagon, pretending it to be for an Englishman to Rietvalley, therefore but one day's journey.
html: The plan being communicated to one Michael Kelly, also an Irishman, he agreed to join, and Hooper hired a wagon, pretending it to be for an Englishman to Rietvalley, therefore but one day's journey.

text: Louis, under advice of Hooper, provided himself with a blue jacket with red collar and cuffs, and two silver epaulets, large and small swords, and ostrich feathers for plumes, and then joined Hooper and Abraham, and Kelly, and a deserted slave they met on the road, and proceeded to Mr. Louw's place, to incite as many as possible in the interior to insurrection and rebellion; and having assembled and armed themselves, to march to Cape Town and take a battery, and demand by letter from the Governor the liberty of the slaves in this colony, to storm the prison and release the prisoners, and to fight for the liberty of the slaves. Louis was to be the governor or chief of the blacks, Hooper to have a high situation, and they expected assistance of some people living five months from Cape Town; but who these were was not ascertained.

Louis was to be the governor or chief of the blacks, Hooper to have a high situation, and they expected assistance of some people living five months from Cape Town; but who these were was not ascertained.

text: At Louw's, Louis put on two gold epaulets, Hooper a silver one, and having with Kelly armed themselves with swords, their first object was to arrest Louw, but he was not at home.
html: At Louw's, Louis put on two gold epaulets, Hooper a silver one, and having with Kelly armed themselves with swords, their first object was to arrest Louw, but he was not at home.

text: Louis was then introduced to Mrs. Louw as a Spanish captain (he had the dark tinge of that nation), and this kind lady gave him plenty of forage for the horses, a good supper, and permitted all to sleep there, showing them their bed-rooms. Mrs. Louw took supper with them, and several inquiries were made about Louw.
html: Louis was then introduced to Mrs. Louw as a Spanish captain (he had the dark tinge of that nation), and this kind lady gave him plenty of forage for the horses, a good supper, and permitted all to sleep there, showing them their bed-rooms. Mrs. Louw took supper with them, and several inquiries were made about Louw.

text: The next morning they were joined by Louw's slaves (ten in number) and a Hottentot, and proceeded then to the place of a Mr. Basson, and caused horses to be put to his wagon, and bound him. Doors were then forced and guns and powder taken, and they stated that it was the Governor's and Fiscal's orders to take all Christians and slaves to Cape Town. Mrs. Basson fortunately escaped, together with a Miss Smit, through a window, and by letting themselves down by a rope.
html: The next morning they were joined by Louw's slaves (ten in number) and a Hottentot, and proceeded then to the place of a Mr. Basson, and caused horses to be put to his wagon, and bound him. Doors were then forced and guns and powder taken, and they stated that it was the Governor's and Fiscal's orders to take all Christians and slaves to Cape Town. Mrs. Basson fortunately escaped, together with a Miss Smit, through a window, and by letting themselves down by a rope.

text: They, now having twelve wagons and four saddle horses, keeping Basson under arrest and having pinioned him on the road, went to the place of another Mr. Louw, seized him, took his money, gun and powder, and armed several of his slaves with swords; also to one Mr. van der Westhuyzen's, committing the same acts, adding wine and clothing to their robbery, and binding him. And here (under a threat whilst holding the muzzle of a gun to the breast and forcing) even an act of ravishment was committed.
html: They, now having twelve wagons and four saddle horses, keeping Basson under arrest and having pinioned him on the road, went to the place of another Mr. Louw, seized him, took his money, gun and powder, and armed several of his slaves with swords; also to one Mr. van der Westhuyzen's, committing the same acts, adding wine and clothing to their robbery, and binding him. And here (under a threat whilst holding the muzzle of a gun to the breast and forcing) even an act of ravishment was committed.

text: The number of insurgents had now so increased that they could be formed into two divisions, and Louis took command of one of them, and they proceeded through Koeberg and Tygerberg, Visserhok and Paalen, visiting in all thirty-four farms, taking with them, the masters and Christians (whites) bound, and their wagons, horses, arms, ammunition, and slaves: holding out to these that they were to be free, committing several outrages, and directing their course towards Salt River, where some poles for the guidance of travellers were planted. This seemed destined as the place of rendezvous.

This seemed destined as the place of rendezvous.

text: The slaves (whom they had induced to follow them partly by force and partly by making them believe were then to be free) cried out every where that such was the order of the Governor, the General, and Fiscal.
html: The slaves (whom they had induced to follow them partly by force and partly by making them believe were then to be free) cried out every where that such was the order of the Governor, the General, and Fiscal.

text: From some places they carried the masters bound, from others unbound, in the charge of armed blacks; at other places they distributed wine among the people, committing great excesses, and under the shouts of huzza and firing (in and outside of the houses), they broke windows, chests, and trunks to pieces, entirely plundering the latter, so that several farmers suffered severely; and the most, one Mr. Christian Storm, of whom not a single slave joined the insurgents, but concealed themselves in the bushes. He was surprised by these men, armed, in the middle of the night in his own house, where they broke open all the chests, trunks, and doors of different rooms, and deprived him of nearly everything that came in their way; and having afterwards bound him, almost naked, as they had taken him out of his bed, they threw him into a wagon; whilst another party committed violence and plunder at a place in the neighbourhood of a Mr. van der Spuy, taking from him his writing desk and papers. They also seized a Mr. Adriaan Louw, of Drooge Valley, a man upwards of seventy years, on his place, and ill-treated him in the highest degree, laying hold of him by his hair, giving him a blow with the but-end of a musket on his head, and beating him with a sword.

They also seized a Mr. Adriaan Louw, of Drooge Valley, a man upwards of seventy years, on his place, and ill-treated him in the highest degree, laying hold of him by his hair, giving him a blow with the but-end of a musket on his head, and beating him with a sword.

text: Some farmers were left behind as prisoners, whilst they proceeded to the place of a Mr. Arend de Waal, at the Paalen, and ill-treated him, taking his guns, and arresting two other farmers Messrs. Joubert and Lategaan, then travelling on the road.
html: Some farmers were left behind as prisoners, whilst they proceeded to the place of a Mr. Arend de Waal, at the Paalen, and ill-treated him, taking his guns, and arresting two other farmers Messrs. Joubert and Lategaan, then travelling on the road.

text: The Governor, Lord Caledon, having received a report of this insurrection on the 27th October, between 9 and 10 o'clock in the evening, had detachments of cavalry and infantry immediately despatched. Some of the parties were apprehended at Blueberg and the Paalen, others at Tygerberg. There were confined at Fort de Knokke, one hundred and twenty-six; at Maastricht at Tygerberg, two hundred; escaped, five; total three hundred and thirty-one. Wagons, horses, guns, &c., were immediately returned to the owners, but a great many articles were lost in the confusion. The five prisoners who had escaped were successively apprehended, and to the masters were returned two hundred and forty-four slaves, and some of the others, who appeared to have been acting passively; and only fifty-one were actually brought to trial, after a preliminary examination.

The five prisoners who had escaped were successively apprehended, and to the masters were returned two hundred and forty-four slaves, and some of the others, who appeared to have been acting passively; and only fifty-one were actually brought to trial, after a preliminary examination.

text: The prisoners consisted to two Europeans, one Hottentot, and forty-eight slaves. Their sentence was pronounced on the 31st of December, 1808. Sixteen were to be hanged, and the bodies of four of them exposed; the others to be scourged, and eight of them exposed with ropes round their necks (punishment next to capital), and twenty-one in addition, branded; besides some who were condemned to the public works for life, twenty-five, fifteen, ten and five years,—three were returned to their masters to work in irons, and four to witness the execution, and be returned to their masters.

text: Ultimately, His Excellency the Governor exercised his power of remitting the punishments, so that nine only were to be executed, the bodies of five exposed, four confined for life, six for fifteen, two for five, and one for three years (after punish¬ment to be returned to their masters), the remainder also after witnessing the punishment. The sentences against one of the Europeans and one of the prisoners (Adonis) condemned to capital punishment were suspended, and ultimately that of Kelly were remitted, but he was sent to England to await His Majesty's pleasure, whilst Adonis was banished for life.

text: Thus ended this melancholy event under a kind Providence, without bloodshed before the apprehension of the prisoners; and fortunately the insurrection extended itself but partially, and was confined to that part of the colony where the slave population was less dense and not so civilized as in other quarters.

text: The sight of so many prisoners, and the proceedings which I read in the office whilst copying some of the examinations and sentences, made a deep impression on my mind, and raised serious thoughts regarding the existence and justice of slavery. For the desire of liberty being the origin of the crimes committed, was (as it struck me) but natural, though at the period of bondage unlawful. The order, peace, and state of society then, however, required severe measures to check further and fatal progress; so they could not be avoided.

text: Proceeding in the office under a cheerful discharge of my duties, and flattering hopes of success, I met in 1809, going one morning to the office (then in the castle), a gentleman (Mr. Francis Dashwood) who had been residing at Stellenbosch for his health when I was a lad learning my Latin lessons. He used to visit my father and observed this, and had the kindness to invite me to his house, and took some interest in my progress. He asked me what prospect I had in the service? I opened to him my views, and he advised me “to continue and endeavour to distinguish myself.”
