text: It so happened that, soon after, Government determined that the Venduemastership1 should not remain attached to the situation of the secretary of Stellenbosch but be separated, and my old friend, Mr. Wege, resolved to be vendue master. Apprised of his intention, I communicated my wishes to succeed him, as secretary, to my friend, Mr. Dashwood. He had the kindness to draw up my memorial; being at that time Receiver-General, he was a man of influence, and by his favourable representation of my case to the Governor, Lord Caledon, the recommendation of the Colonial Secretary, Mr. Alexander, and the testimonial of my superiors I succeeded in obtaining that situation, and received my appointment, dated 18th December, 1809. This promotion was a great step, for, besides being allowed a house and garden, my salary amounted to £75, with fees, and I was the only notary ex officio in the district.

text: Dat nu omtrend thien dagen verleeden des avonds wanneer des relatants lijfheer niet thuijs en haar lijfvrouw reeds te bed gegaan was, terwijl zij nevens de mede slavinne Candace, den slaaf Julij en zijn zoontje Februarij, zig in de combuijs ter harer lijfheers plaats bevonden, gem. Februarij de slavinne Cadace [sic] over haar krom Duijts spreeken bespot en uitgelagt mitsgds. dat jongetje van meerm. Julij daarover bestraft en een á twee klappen om de ooren gekreegen had, was den aldaar als knegt wonenden burger Michiel Radijn daar bij gekomen en had tegens ged. Julij gesegd, waarom hij gerepte slave jongetje voor niet quam te slaan?  Op ’twelke meerm. Julij g’antwoord hebbende: Ik mag hem slaan als hij stout is, ’t is mijn kind, en als de baas hier bij was, zoude hij zeggen, Raak wat.  Zig voorts omme keerende, had hij Radijn een stuk brandhoud [sic] opgenomen en gesz. slaaf Julij daarmede van agteren een slag toegebragt, waarop denselven plotselings ter aarde gevallen zijnde, dusdanig ook was blijven leggen zonder ten eersten van zelfs op te staan, terwijl het gem. stuk hout door midden gebroken zijnde, gem. Radijn de helfte daarvan in de hand quam te houden.

Statement given on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, Marthinus Adrianus, Bergh by the woman slave Dina van de Caab, of competent age, belonging to the burgher Jacobus Malan, being of the following content, namely:
html: Statement given on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, Marthinus Adrianus, Bergh by the woman slave Dina van de Caab, of competent age, belonging to the burgher Jacobus Malan, being of the following content, namely:

text: That about ten days ago now, during the evening, when the owner of the testifier was not at home and her mistress had already gone to bed, and while she, as also her fellow woman slave Candace, the slave Julij and his little son Februarij, were in the kitchen on her owner’s farm, the said Februarij was ridiculing and laughing at the woman slave Candace because of her speaking broken Dutch, and moreover that this little boy received as punishment for this a clout or two on the ears from the aforementioned Julij, which is when the burgher Michiel Radijn, who lives there as knecht, came in and asked the said July why he was beating the little boy for nothing? To which the aforementioned Julij answered: “I may beat him when he is naughty, he is my child, and if the baas were here, he would have said: ‘Go on, hit him!’”. When he [Julij] then turned around, Radijn took up a piece of fire wood and gave the said slave Julij a blow with it from behind, whereupon he instantly fell to the ground, and remained lying like this without at once getting up by himself, while the said piece of wood broke in the middle, with Radijn holding the one half of it in his hand.

To which the aforementioned Julij answered: “I may beat him when he is naughty, he is my child, and if the baas were here, he would have said: ‘Go on, hit him!’”. Relaas gegeven ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, door de slavinne Candace van de Caab van competenten ouderdom, toebehorende den burger Jacobus Malan, zijnde van den volgenden inhoud, namentlijk:
html: Relaas gegeven ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, door de slavinne Candace van de Caab van competenten ouderdom, toebehorende den burger Jacobus Malan, zijnde van den volgenden inhoud, namentlijk:

text: Dat nu eenige dagen geleeden wanneer de relatante ter harer lijfheers plaats des avonds in de combuijs was en zij door seeker slave jongetje Februarij gent., onder het spreken van een Duijts woord door haar niet wel uitgebragt, telkens bespot en uitgelagt werdenden, den slaaf Julij (zijnde de vader van dat jongetje) hem daar over bestraft en twee klappen gegeven had, was den knegt Michiel Radijn daar bij gekomenen gem. Julij gevraagd hebbende waarom hij Februarij voor niet quam te slaan? Denselven daarop had g’antwoord: Ik mag hem slaan, ’t is mijn kind, als de baas hier bij was zoude hij zeggen Raak wat, waarop meerm. Julij zig had omgekeerd terwijl voorsz. Radijn een stuk brandhoud [sic] opgenomen, en denselven Julij daarmede van agteren een slag had toegebragt, dermaten dat dien jongen daarop plotselings ter aarde was komen te vallen, terwijl dat gem. stuk houd onder ’t slaan door midden gebroken waarvan d’ helfte op den grond gevallen weesende, gem. Radijn ’t ander gedeelte in de hand behield.

text: That some days ago now, during the evening, when the testifier was in the kitchen on her owner’s farm and was continually being ridiculed and laughed at by a certain little slave boy named February whenever she said a Dutch word not well pronounced by her, the slave Julij (being the father of this little boy) punished him for this and gave him two clouts, when the knecht Michiel Radijn came in and asked the said Julij why he beat Februarij for nothing?, who replied to this: “I may beat him, he is my child, if the baas were here, he would have said: ‘Go on, hit him!’”. Whereupon the aforementioned Julij turned himself around, while aforesaid Radijn took up a piece of fire wood and gave the same Julij a blow with it from the back, in such a way that this jongen thereupon came to fall down to the ground suddenly, while that piece of wood broke in the middle during the blow, of which the one half fell to the ground, while the said Radijn held the other piece in his hand.

text: Dat op seekere dag die den compt. niet wist te noemen, des avonds eer het donker was geworden, wanneer den compt. ter zijner lijfheer plaats, naar de fontein om water voor zig in een ketel te halen gegaan en bij de aldaar staande vijgeboom gekomen was, van nabij had gezien dat gem. zijnen lijfheer en desselfs dogter Elsie onder gem. boom op elkanderen gelegen zijnde te samen deeden als man en vrouw.  Waarop den compt. uit vreese van door zijnen baas gesien te werden, zig in den wijngaard had gaan verschuijlen totdat zij beide opgestaan en van daar vertrokken waren, als wanneer hij compt. zijn ketel met water had gevuld en voorts wederom naar huijs gegaan was.

text: That in the evening, before it had become dark, of a certain day, which he cannot name, when the testifier went to the fountain on his owner’s farm to fetch water in a kettle for himself and reached the fig tree standing there, he saw from close by that his said owner and the latter’s daughter Elsie were lying on each other under the said tree and were doing with each other as husband and wife. Whereupon the testifier, from fear of being seen by his baas, hid in the vineyard until they both got up and departed from there, which is when he filled his kettle with water and went back to the house.

Huijden den 14e Junij 1775 compareerde voor mij Abraham Faure, secrets. van Stellenbosch en Drakenstein, present de nagen. getuijgen, den burger Gideon van Zijl Pz. van competenten ouderdom, denwelken ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, verklaarde hoe waar is:
html: Huijden den 14e Junij 1775 compareerde voor mij Abraham Faure, secrets. van Stellenbosch en Drakenstein, present de nagen. getuijgen, den burger Gideon van Zijl Pz. van competenten ouderdom, denwelken ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, verklaarde hoe waar is:

text: Dat wanneer den compt. in ’t begin der jongst gepasseerde maand Maij, zijnde hem den juiste datum ontschoten, met zijne vader des nagts ter plaats van den veldcorporaal Gerrit Smit geleegen aan de Picquet Bergen, gekomen en hun osse wagen aldaar uitgespannen waren den compt. des morgens met gem. Smit naar ’t aldaar staande molenhuijs, dat dien nagt door eenige drossers opengebroken was, gegaan zijnde, zijl. bevonden hadden, dat ’t venster van het vertrek ingebroken was, mitsgds. dat twee aldaar gestaan hebbende mudden meel op den grond uitgestort, en de sakken met circa een halve mud meel gestolen waren.  Dat den compt. nevens gem. Smit zig daarop in ’t voorm. gebergte ter opspeuringe der sporen dier vagebonden gegaan dog niets daarvan ontdekt hebbende, des middags teruggekomen waren.  Dat den compt. na ’t middagmaal zig alleen omstreeks voorm. plaats ter opspeuringe als voren begeven en eenige sporen ontdekt had, waarop den compt. weder naar ’t huijs gegaan en voorsz. Smit sulx gesegd  hebbende.  Waren zij beijde vervolgens die sporen nagegaan, ieder met een roer dat met grof hagel geladen was, gewapend, terwijl den compt. den bij zijn wagen bescheijden zijnde Bastaard Hottentot Gerrit Obie, die alleenlijk een kirrij bij zig had, met hun had doen mede gaan, waarna zijl. seekere Hottentot Jan gent. (die hun quam waarschouwen dat hij eenige sporen had gezien) ontmoetende, denselven mede bij zig gehouden hadden, als wanneer zijl. de gevonden sporen agtervolgd hebbende, omtrent den oever eener droge rivier gekomen, en voor een aldaar staande bosch, eenige kleederen ontwaard hadden, terwijl voorsz. Smit ’t eerst quam t’ ontdekken, dat ’er in dat bosch eenige drossers op den grond lagen. Waarop hij Smit hun toegeroepen en gevraagd hebbende wiens slaven zij waren met bijvoeging, dat zijl. uitkomen en zig gevangen overgeven moesten, alstoen met hun vieren ieder met blote messen en een hertsvanger in de handen ten voorschijn quamen, posseerende zig voor dat bosch, op ’twelke hun door gem. veldcorp. Smit een en andermaal toegeroepen zijnde, dat zij hun scherp wegwerpen en zig overgeven moesten, waren zij gesamentlijk zonder ’t minste antwoord te hebben gegeven, met hun scherp op den compt. en gem. Smit komen t’ advanceeren, waarop ged. Smit hun, onder bedreiging van op hun te zullen schieten, had gewaarschouwd te blijven staan, hun scherp weg te gooijen en alsdan een voor een bij hem te komen, waarna zijl. zonder zig van hunnen messen en hertsvanger t’ ontdoen, egter bleven staan.  Dat na een wijle tijds hun als voren gesegt zijnde zig zonder scherp gevangen te geeven, zonder dat zijl. er op quamen t’ antwoorden, dog onder elkanderen in hunne taal spraken, en dus bleven staan, had voorsz. Smit den compt. gecommandeert om een dier drossers naar de beenen te schieten zeggende dat zij zig dan wel gevangen geeven zouden, waarop hij compt. een derselve door een rietpol waar denselven agter stond naar de beenen geschoten hebbende, gem. jongen terstond neder gevallen was, terwijl de andere drie aanstonds daarop met hun scherp op hem quamen inlopen onder ’t roepen van: Amok Amok! waarna den compt. zig op ’t lopen geset hebbende, voorm. Smit een dier jongens die hem compt. het naast agter ’t lijf was, zodanig met een schoot had getroffen, dat opstonds dood ter aarde was komen neder te vallen; zijnde de twee overige toen met hunne messen op gem. Smit ingekomen, die zig mede ter vlugt moeste begeven, vermits zijn geweer nog niet geladen was, op ’twelke, nadat den comp. weder een schoot in den loop op een dier beijde jongens had gedaan zonder denselven geraakt te hebben, zijl. zig voorts wederom naar ’t voorsz. bosch hadden begeven, terwijl Smit en den compt. hunne geweers weder geladen en vervolgens die twee drossers agtervolgd hadden.  Dat deselve alstoen op de aankomst van den compt. en Smit zig ter vlugt over meerm. rivier hadden begeven, wanneer gerepte Smit de oudste dier slaven agterhaald en toegeroepen had van zijne beijde in handen hebbende messen weg te werpen en zig gevangen te geven, ged. slaaf maar een derselve naar hem Smit had toegeworpen, waarna hij Smit naar de anderen gelopen zijnde, den compt. en voorsz. Gerrit den evengem. oude slaaf, nadat hij ’t ander mes had weggeworpen, gevangen hadden genomen; terwijl meerm. Smit den anderen agterhaald en hem als voren toegeroepen had zijn scherp weg te gooijen en zig gevangen te geven, denselven, onder ’t roepen: Bie! Bie! op hem Smit met ’t scherp was aangekomen, waarop hij Smit geretireerd zijnde, en nogmaals hem het vorige toegeroepen hebbende, zonder dat ged. slaaf zig des bekreunde, had voorm. Smit denselven met een kogel dermaten door ’t lijf geschoten, dat terstonds was komen neder te vallen, dog zig te vergeefs hebbende willen opregten, was denselven met ’t mes in de hand komen te sterven.
html: Dat wanneer den compt. in ’t begin der jongst gepasseerde maand Maij, zijnde hem den juiste datum ontschoten, met zijne vader des nagts ter plaats van den veldcorporaal Gerrit Smit geleegen aan de Picquet Bergen, gekomen en hun osse wagen aldaar uitgespannen waren den compt. des morgens met gem. Dat den compt. na ’t middagmaal zig alleen omstreeks voorm. plaats ter opspeuringe als voren begeven en eenige sporen ontdekt had, waarop den compt. weder naar ’t huijs gegaan en voorsz. Smit sulx gesegd hebbende. Waren zij beijde vervolgens die sporen nagegaan, ieder met een roer dat met grof hagel geladen was, gewapend, terwijl den compt. den bij zijn wagen bescheijden zijnde Bastaard Hottentot Gerrit Obie, die alleenlijk een kirrij bij zig had, met hun had doen mede gaan, waarna zijl. seekere Hottentot Jan gent. (die hun quam waarschouwen dat hij eenige sporen had gezien) ontmoetende, denselven mede bij zig gehouden hadden, als wanneer zijl. de gevonden sporen agtervolgd hebbende, omtrent den oever eener droge rivier gekomen, en voor een aldaar staande bosch, eenige kleederen ontwaard hadden, terwijl voorsz. text: TRANSLATION

Today, 14 June1775, there appears before me, Abraham Faure, secretary of Stellenbosch and Drakenstein, in the presence of the witnesses named below, the burgher Gideon van Zijl Pz., of competent age, who on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, declares it to be true:
html: Today, 14 June1775, there appears before me, Abraham Faure, secretary of Stellenbosch and Drakenstein, in the presence of the witnesses named below, the burgher Gideon van Zijl Pz., of competent age, who on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, declares it to be true:

text: That at the beginning of the recently passed month of May, although the exact date has slipped his mind, the testifier came at night with his father to the farm of the veldcorporaal Gerrit Smit, situated at Piketberg, and out spanned their ox wagon there. In the morning when the testifier went with the said Smit to the mill there, which had been broken into by deserters that night, they found that the window of the room had been broken open and also that two mudden flour which had been stored there, was spilled on the ground and that the bags, with about half a mud of flour, had been stolen. That the testifier then went with the said Smit to the aforementioned mountain in order to find the traces of these vagabonds but could not discover anything and returned at noon. That after lunch the testifier went on his own to the aforementioned place in order to search as before and discovered some traces, whereupon the testifier again went to the house and informed the aforesaid Smit of this. Both of them then followed these traces, each armed with a gun loaded with small shot, while the testifier made the Bastaard-Hottentot Gerrit Obie, who was assigned to his wagon and who only had a kirrij with him, come with them. After they met up with a certain Hottentot named Jan (who came to warn them that he had seen some traces) they also kept him with them, which is when they followed the traces they found until they came to the banks of a dry river and noticed some clothes lying in front of a bush there, while the aforesaid Smit was the first to discover that there were also some deserters lying on the ground by that bush. Hereupon he, Smit, called to them and asked them whose slaves they were, adding that they should come out and give themselves up as prisoners, which is when the four of them came forward, each holding an unsheathed knife and one a cutlass in their hands, drawing themselves up in front of that bush. When the said veldcorporaal Smit once or twice called to them that they should throw down their knives and surrender, they all, without giving the least answer, advanced together with their knives towards the testifier and the said Smit, whereupon the said Smit warned them, under threat of shooting at them, to remain standing, to throw down their knives and to come to him one-by-one; which is when they, without however ridding themselves of their knives and cutlass, stopped. That after a short while they were told, as before, to give themselves up as prisoners without their knives; yet they did not answer to this, talked amongst themselves in their language, and remained standing like this. The aforesaid Smit then ordered the testifier to shoot one of these deserters in his legs, saying that they would then give themselves up as prisoners, whereupon the testifier shot at the legs of one of them through a clump of reeds behind which the same was standing, when the said jongen immediately fell down, whereupon the other three instantly rushed towards them with their knives while shouting: “Amok, amok!”. At this, the testifier started running away, which is when the aforesaid Smit hit one of these jongens, who was the closest behind the testifier, with a shot in such a way that he instantly fell down dead to the ground. The two remaining ones then ran with their knives towards the said Smit, who also had to take flight as his gun had not yet been reloaded. After this, when the testifier had again, while running, shot at one of these jongens, without hitting them, they once again went to the aforesaid bush, while Smit and the testifier reloaded their guns, after which they followed these two deserters. The same then, on the arrival of the testifier and Smit, took flight across the aforementioned river, which is when the said Smit caught up with the oldest of these slaves and called at him to throw down the knives which he held in both his hands and to give himself up as prisoner, but instead of that, the said slave threw one of them at Smit, after which Smit ran after the other one, while the testifier and the aforesaid Gerrit took the said old slave prisoner, after he had thrown down his other knife. In the meantime, the aforementioned Smit caught up with the other one and, as before, called to him to throw down his knives and to give himself up as prisoner, when the same, while calling: “Come, come”, rushed towards Smit with the knives, whereupon Smit retreated and yet again called the aforesaid to him, without the said slave caring much for this, which is when the aforementioned Smit shot him with a bullet through his body in such a way that he immediately fell down, but in vain attempted to lift himself up and died holding the knife in his hand.

text: That the testifier again went with the aforementioned Smit to the aforesaid bush where they found the two stolen bags with fully half a mud of flour as well as four knives, and understood from the old slave that they were slaves of the fabricq at the Cape.

Huijden den 14 Junij 1775 compareerde voor mij Abraham Faure, secret., van Stellenbosch en Drakenstein, present de nagen. getuijgen, den Bastaard Hottentot Gerrit Obie, van competenten ouderdom, denwelken ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, verklaarde hoe waar is:
html: Huijden den 14 Junij 1775 compareerde voor mij Abraham Faure, secret., van Stellenbosch en Drakenstein, present de nagen. getuijgen, den Bastaard Hottentot Gerrit Obie, van competenten ouderdom, denwelken ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, verklaarde hoe waar is:

text: Dat den compt. in huur zijnde bij den burger Andries Greef, enigen tijd voorz. zonder die te kunnen bepalen, met een wagen van den medeburger Pieter van Zijl die nevens zijn zoon Gideon van Zijl op deselven wagen, des nagts ter plaats van den veldcorporaal Gerrit Smit gekomen en aldaar de beesten uitgespannen, terwijl men des volgende morgens vernam dat het molenhuijs ter gem. plaats dien nagt opengebroken was, gem. Smit en Gideon van Zijl des morgens nadat zij het gem. molenhuijs hadden gaan bezigtigen, vervolgens zig naar ’t gebergte begeven om de sporen van de drossers op te soeken, waarna zij des middags weder terug gekomen waren zonder eenige sporen te hebben gevonden, dat na het eeten, door Gideon van Zijl beneden ’t huijs eenige sporen ontdekt zijnde, denselven vervolgens met voorn. Gerrit Smit, ieder met een snaphaan gewapend, en den compt. met een kirrij, de gevondene sporen nagegaan waren, ontmoetende den Hottentot Jan, die ook eenige sporen ontdekt had, zijnde zijl. dus tesamen de sporen vervolgende, gekomen omtrent een droge rivier alwaar zijl. bij een bosch eenige kleederen zagen leggen, waarna den veldcorporaal Smit eenige jongens in ’t bosch leggende ontdekt en deselven toegeroepen had, dat zij uit komen en zig gevangen geven moesten, waarop vier slaven voort quamen ieder met bloote messen en een derselver met een hertsvanger in hunne handen (terwijl den Hottentot Jan naar de rivier was gegaan om een stok voor zig te halen) op ’twelke den veldcorporaal voorsz. jongens tot drie á vier maal toegeroepen hebbende dat zij hun scherp zouden weggooijen en zig gevangen geeven, hetgeen zij niet hadden willen doen, hij Smit door gem. Gideon van Zijl een van die drossers naar de beenen had laten schieten, ’twelk gedaan en den geschoten jongen, die d’ hertevanger in handen had nedergevallen zijnde, waren de andere drie op gem. van Zijl komen inlopen met het scherp in de handen, waarop Gerrit Smit een dier jongens die ’t naaste agter van Zijl was, heeft doodgeschoten, waarna de twee overige op Smit quamen aan zetten, den welken zig mede op den loop begeven hebbende, had gerepte van Zijl wederom naar een van hun geschoten dog niet geraaken, waarop gem. twee jongens omgekeerd en over de rivier gevlugt waren, komende gem. Smit de oude jongen te agterhalen denwelken op ’t geroep van Smit een zijner messen naar denselven quam te werpen, terwijl hij ’t ander in zijn hand hield, waarop meerm. Smit den anderen slaaf vervolgd en agterhaald hebbende, terwijl denselven alweder met ’t scherp op hem quam aanlopen, doodgeschoten had, hebbende den <andere>  de laatsten van hun reeds zijn mes weggeworpen en zig toen gevangen gegeven.

text: TRANSLATION

Today, 14 June1775, there appears before me, Abraham Faure, secretary of Stellenbosch and Drakenstein, in the presence of the witnesses named below, the Bastaard-Hottentot Gerrit Obie, of competent age, who on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, declares it to be true:
html: Today, 14 June1775, there appears before me, Abraham Faure, secretary of Stellenbosch and Drakenstein, in the presence of the witnesses named below, the Bastaard-Hottentot Gerrit Obie, of competent age, who on the requisition of the honourable landdrost, Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, declares it to be true:

text: That some time ago, without being able to determine when, the testifier, who is hired by the burgher Andries Greef, came by night with a wagon of the burgher Pieter van Zijl, who was with his son Gideon van Zijl on the same wagon, to the farm of the veldcorporaal Gerrit Smit and out spanned the oxen there. Since they learned the following morning that the mill on the said farm had been broken into that night, the said Smit and Gideon van Zijl, after they had inspected the mill that morning, went to the mountain to look for traces of deserters, after which they returned again at noon without having found any traces. That after lunch Gideon van Zijl discovered some traces below the house, and that the same then, with the aforementioned Gerrit Smit, each armed with a musket, and the testifier with a kirrij, followed the traces and met up with the Hottentot Jan, who had also discovered some traces, after which they all followed the traces together until they came in the vicinity of a dry river where they saw some clothes lying by a bush. Hereafter the veldcorporaal Smit discovered some jongens lying by the bush and called to them that they should come out and give themselves up as prisoners, whereupon four slaves came forward, each with unsheathed knives and one of them with a cutlass in their hands (while the Hottentot Jan had gone to the river to fetch a stick for himself), upon which the veldcorporaal called three or four times to the aforesaid jongens that they should throw down their knives and should give themselves up as prisoners, which they did not want to do. Smit then told Gideon van Zijl to shoot one of these deserters in his legs, which he did and when the shot jongen, who had the cutlass in his hand, fell down, the other three came running to the said van Zijl with the knives in their hands, whereupon Gerrit Smit shot dead one of these jongens who was the closest behind van Zijl. After this the two remaining rushed towards Smit, who also started running away, when the said van Zijl again shot at one of them, yet without hitting, whereupon the said two jongens turned around and fled over the river. The said Smit was catching up with the older jongen who, when Smit called out, threw one of his knives at the same, while he held the other one in his hand, whereupon the aforementioned Smit, having continued after the other slave and caught up with him and, while the same again rushed towards him with his knife, shot him dead; meanwhile the last of them had already thrown away his knife and then gave himself up as prisoner.

heading: 1775 — Crime Records (Slaves: Moses van de Caab)
text: 1775 — Crime Records (Slaves: Moses van de Caab)
html: 1775 — Crime Records (Slaves: Moses van de Caab)

text: Nademaal Moses van de Caab slaaf van de wed. wijlen den burger Christoffel Groenewald, oud naar gissing 30 jaaren, thans ’s heeren gevn., vrijwillig beleeden heeft, en den E. Agtb. Raad van Justitie deeses gouvernements uijt de verder ten processe gevoegde stukken evident gebleeken is:
html: Nademaal Moses van de Caab slaaf van de wed. wijlen den burger Christoffel Groenewald, oud naar gissing 30 jaaren, thans ’s heeren gevn., vrijwillig beleeden heeft, en den E. Agtb. Raad van Justitie deeses gouvernements uijt de verder ten processe gevoegde stukken evident gebleeken is:

text: Dat wanneer den gevn., ter sijner lijfvrouwen plaatse, geleegen bij Stellenbosch, nu wel een maand voorleeden, op een voordemiddag, neevens eenige sijner meede slaaven jongens October en Januarij, in den wijngaard met druijven te snijden beesig geweest was, en om deselve naar den kelder te transporteeren, op een, ten dien eijnde, bij den wijngaard staanden waagen, gelaaden waaren, terwijl den gevn. soo wel als den meede slaaf October onder ’t spannen der beesten, voor den wagen, ieder een paar ossen, aan een riem gebonden, aan de hand gehad, en vast gehouden hadden; den gevn. en voorsz. October intusschen eenig verschil hadden bekoomen; ter saake voorsz. October tot den gevn. gesegt hebbende dat hij gevn. de beesten wat uijt den weg trecken moest, opdat deselve hem October niet quaamen te schoppen, den gevn., naar daarop onder anderen geantwoord te hebben: Dat kan ik niet doen! voorts in quaadheijd, den meedeslaaf Januarij, die omtrent ses treeden, ter seijden agter hem stond, onder ’t uijtten van onbetamelijke bewoordingen, toegeroepen had: Jaag de ossen aan!
html: Dat wanneer den gevn., ter sijner lijfvrouwen plaatse, geleegen bij Stellenbosch, nu wel een maand voorleeden, op een voordemiddag, neevens eenige sijner meede slaaven jongens October en Januarij, in den wijngaard met druijven te snijden beesig geweest was, en om deselve naar den kelder te transporteeren, op een, ten dien eijnde, bij den wijngaard staanden waagen, gelaaden waaren, terwijl den gevn. soo wel als den meede slaaf October onder ’t spannen der beesten, voor den wagen, ieder een paar ossen, aan een riem gebonden, aan de hand gehad, en vast gehouden hadden; den gevn. en voorsz. October intusschen eenig verschil hadden bekoomen; ter saake voorsz. October tot den gevn. gesegt hebbende dat hij gevn. de beesten wat uijt den weg trecken moest, opdat deselve hem October niet quaamen te schoppen, den gevn., naar daarop onder anderen geantwoord te hebben: Dat kan ik niet doen! voorts in quaadheijd, den meedeslaaf Januarij, die omtrent ses treeden, ter seijden agter hem stond, onder ’t uijtten van onbetamelijke bewoordingen, toegeroepen had: Jaag de ossen aan!

text: Dat voorsz. Januarij sulx niet wel verstaan, en door onnooselheijd ’tselve niet schielijk genoeg gedaan hebbende, den gevn. sijnen toorn den ruijmen teugel gevierd, sijn boslemmer mes, steekende in de scheede, uijt sijn broekssak gehaald, de scheede bij de punt gevat, en dat mes met de scheede, soodanig naar gem. Januarij geworpen had, dat het mes uijt de scheede gevloogen sijnde, meerm. Januarij daar door dermaaten in het slinkerbeen getroffen was; dat dien jongen, uijt dat been sterk bloedende, opstonds ter aarde was needergevallen; des de andere slaven, meerm. Januarij van de aarde opgenoomen, op den wagen gelegt, en naar huijs gebragt hadden; alwaar gem. Januarij dan ook eenige wijnige dagen daarna is koomen te overleijden. Sijnde bij chirurgicaale visitatie bevonden geworden, dat meerm. Januarij door dat mes eene wonde voor aan het slinkerbeen, omtrent het scheenbeen, bijna twee handen breed onder het knie, ter diepte van ruijm drie vingeren breed, bekoomen had; waardoor de arteria of groote ader, ten eenemaal af gesneeden geweest was; invoegen den gevn. ten eersten gevat, naar Stellenbosch gebragt, en van daar Caabwaards in handen van Justitie overgeleevert geworden is.
html: Dat voorsz. Januarij sulx niet wel verstaan, en door onnooselheijd ’tselve niet schielijk genoeg gedaan hebbende, den gevn. sijnen toorn den ruijmen teugel gevierd, sijn boslemmer mes, steekende in de scheede, uijt sijn broekssak gehaald, de scheede bij de punt gevat, en dat mes met de scheede, soodanig naar gem. Januarij geworpen had, dat het mes uijt de scheede gevloogen sijnde, meerm. Sijnde bij chirurgicaale visitatie bevonden geworden, dat meerm. text: Maar nademaal diergelijken quaadaardigen gedoente en daaruijt geproflueerde quetsing in een land alwaar regt en geregtigheijd gehandhaaft word, geensins ongepunieert gelaaten werden kan, maar ten voorbeelde en afschrik van andere gestraft werden moet.
html: Maar nademaal diergelijken quaadaardigen gedoente en daaruijt geproflueerde quetsing in een land alwaar regt en geregtigheijd gehandhaaft word, geensins ongepunieert gelaaten werden kan, maar ten voorbeelde en afschrik van andere gestraft werden moet.

text: Soo is ’t dat den E. Agtb. Raad van Justitie voorm., ten dage dienende, met nadruk geleesen en overwoogen hebbende, den schriftelijken crimineelen eijsch ende conclusie, door den landdrost van Stellenbosch en Drakensteijn Sr. Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, nomine officii, op ende jeegens den gevn. gedaan ende genoomen, mitsgs. geleth op des gevs. vrijwillige confessien en andere stucken daarneevens gevoegt, alle in judicio behoorlijk gerecolleert, voorts op alle hetgeene ter saake dienende was, en haar E. Agtbs. eenigsints konde doen moveeren regt doende uijt naame ende van weegens de hoogmoogende Heeren Staaten Generaal der Vereenigde Neederlanden den gevn. Moses van de Caab hebben gecondemneert, gelijk haar E. Agtbs. deselve condemneere mits deesen, omme gebragt te werden ter plaatse alwaar men alhier gewoon is, crimineele gewijsdens te executeeren, aldaar den scherpregter overgeleevert, en aan een paal gebonden, mitsgaders met roeden op de bloote rugge strengelijk gegeesselt sijnde; vervolgens den tijd van vijf en twintig agter een volgende jaaren, op het Robben Eijland aan ’s E. Compies. gemeene werken te arbeijden, met condemnatie in de kosten en misen van justitie, ontseggende den Raad den verderen gedaanen eijsch van den officier.

text: Aldus gedaan en gesententieert in ’t Casteel de Goede Hoop den 20 April 1775, mitsgs. gepronuntieert ende geëxecuteert den 29e daaraanvolgende.
html: Aldus gedaan en gesententieert in ’t Casteel de Goede Hoop den 20 April 1775, mitsgs. gepronuntieert ende geëxecuteert den 29e daaraanvolgende.

text: Fiat Executie,
[get.] Jm. van Plettenberg.
TRANSLATION

Since Moses van de Caab, slave of the widow of the late burgher Christoffel Groenewald, 30 years old at a guess, currently their honours’ prisoner, has voluntarily confessed and since, from the other documents produced in the case, it has appeared evident to the honourable Council of Justice of this government:
html: Since Moses van de Caab, slave of the widow of the late burgher Christoffel Groenewald, 30 years old at a guess, currently their honours’ prisoner, has voluntarily confessed and since, from the other documents produced in the case, it has appeared evident to the honourable Council of Justice of this government:

text: That now fully a month ago, during the late morning, when the prisoner was busy harvesting grapes in the vineyard on his owner’s farm, situated in Stellenbosch, with his fellow slave jongens October and Januarij and, in order to transport the grapes to the cellar, was loading them onto a wagon which stood by the vineyard for this purpose; while the prisoner, as well as his fellow slave October, during their spanning in of the cattle before the wagon, each had on his hands a couple of oxen tied to a rope which they held tight, the prisoner and the aforesaid October during this developed some disagreement, in the course of which the aforesaid October said to the prisoner that he should move the cattle out of the way so that they would not kick him, October. The prisoner, after inter alia answering to this: “I cannot do that!”, also called out in anger (while uttering indecent words) to his fellow slave, Januarij, who stood about six steps to the side behind him: “Drive the oxen forward!”
html: That now fully a month ago, during the late morning, when the prisoner was busy harvesting grapes in the vineyard on his owner’s farm, situated in Stellenbosch, with his fellow slave jongens October and Januarij and, in order to transport the grapes to the cellar, was loading them onto a wagon which stood by the vineyard for this purpose; while the prisoner, as well as his fellow slave October, during their spanning in of the cattle before the wagon, each had on his hands a couple of oxen tied to a rope which they held tight, the prisoner and the aforesaid October during this developed some disagreement, in the course of which the aforesaid October said to the prisoner that he should move the cattle out of the way so that they would not kick him, October. The prisoner, after inter alia answering to this: “I cannot do that!”, also called out in anger (while uttering indecent words) to his fellow slave, Januarij, who stood about six steps to the side behind him: “Drive the oxen forward!”

text: That as the aforementioned Januarij did not understand this very well, and through ignorance did not do so quickly enough, the prisoner gave full reins to his anger, drew his boslemmer knife in its sheath from the pocket of his trousers, took the sheath by the point and threw the knife in its sheath in such a way to the said Januarij that the knife flew from the sheath and hit the aforementioned Januarij in such a manner in his left leg that this jongen bled heavily from that leg and immediately fell to the ground. The other slaves picked up the aforementioned Januarij from the ground, laid him on the wagon and brought him home, where the said Januarij died a few days thereafter.
html: That as the aforementioned Januarij did not understand this very well, and through ignorance did not do so quickly enough, the prisoner gave full reins to his anger, drew his boslemmer knife in its sheath from the pocket of his trousers, took the sheath by the point and threw the knife in its sheath in such a way to the said Januarij that the knife flew from the sheath and hit the aforementioned Januarij in such a manner in his left leg that this jongen bled heavily from that leg and immediately fell to the ground. The other slaves picked up the aforementioned Januarij from the ground, laid him on the wagon and brought him home, where the said Januarij died a few days thereafter.

text: During his investigation the surgeon found that the aforementioned Januarij received from that knife a wound in the front of his left leg, around the shin-bone, almost two hands below the knee, fully three fingers deep; as a result of which the arteria or great vein was totally severed; so that the prisoner was immediately taken and brought to Stellenbosch and from there to the Cape where he was delivered into the hands of justice.
html: During his investigation the surgeon found that the aforementioned Januarij received from that knife a wound in the front of his left leg, around the shin-bone, almost two hands below the knee, fully three fingers deep; as a result of which the arteria or great vein was totally severed; so that the prisoner was immediately taken and brought to Stellenbosch and from there to the Cape where he was delivered into the hands of justice.

text: But since such evil deeds and the wounding which came of it cannot under any circumstances be left unpunished in a country where law and justice are upheld, but should be punished as an example and a deterrent to others.
html: But since such evil deeds and the wounding which came of it cannot under any circumstances be left unpunished in a country where law and justice are upheld, but should be punished as an example and a deterrent to others.

text: Thus it is, that the honourable Council of Justice, aforementioned, serving today, having read and considered with care the written crimineelen eijsch ende conclusie drawn up and delivered by the landdrost of Stellenbosch and Drakenstein, Sieur Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, in his official capacity, for and against the prisoner, as well as having noted the prisoner’s voluntary confession and the other documents added to it, all properly verified in court, and further everything that served the case and could possibly move their honourables, practising justice in the name and on behalf of the high and mighty Lords States General of the United Netherlands, having judged the prisoner Moses van de Caab, is sentencing him with this: to be taken to the place where criminal sentences are usually executed here, there to be handed over to the executioner and to be tied to a stake; moreover to be severely scourged on the naked back with whips, thereupon to serve for a period of twenty five consecutive years on the honourable Company’s public works on Robben Island, with sentencing to the costs and expenditures of justice; the Council denying the otherwise drawn-up eijsch of the officer [of justice].
html: Thus it is, that the honourable Council of Justice, aforementioned, serving today, having read and considered with care the written crimineelen eijsch ende conclusie drawn up and delivered by the landdrost of Stellenbosch and Drakenstein, Sieur Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, in his official capacity, for and against the prisoner, as well as having noted the prisoner’s voluntary confession and the other documents added to it, all properly verified in court, and further everything that served the case and could possibly move their honourables, practising justice in the name and on behalf of the high and mighty Lords States General of the United Netherlands, having judged the prisoner Moses van de Caab, is sentencing him with this: to be taken to the place where criminal sentences are usually executed here, there to be handed over to the executioner and to be tied to a stake; moreover to be severely scourged on the naked back with whips, thereupon to serve for a period of twenty five consecutive years on the honourable Company’s public works on Robben Island, with sentencing to the costs and expenditures of justice; the Council denying the otherwise drawn-up eijsch of the officer [of justice].

text: Thus done and sentenced in the Castle of Good Hope on 20 April 1775, as also pronounced and executed on the 29th thereupon.
html: Thus done and sentenced in the Castle of Good Hope on 20 April 1775, as also pronounced and executed on the 29th thereupon.

text: Let the sentence be done!
[signed] Jm. van Plettenberg.

Huijden den 13 Maij 1776 compareerde voor mij Abraham Faure secretaris van Stellenbosch en Drakenstein present de nagem. getuijgen, den burger Johan Hendrik Ehlers van competenten ouderdom, denwelken ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Marthinus Adrianus Bergh verklaard hoe waar is:
html: Huijden den 13 Maij 1776 compareerde voor mij Abraham Faure secretaris van Stellenbosch en Drakenstein present de nagem. getuijgen, den burger Johan Hendrik Ehlers van competenten ouderdom, denwelken ter requisitie van den heer landdrost Marthinus Adrianus Bergh verklaard hoe waar is:

text: Dat wanneer den compt. op Vrijdag den 20 der gepasseerde maand April zig aan Cabo bevonden had, den burger Coenraad Eb hem aldaar hadde verhaald, dat den van ’s compts. plaats weggelopenen en vervolgens aan de Caab gevangenen slaaf Julij des avonds voordat denselven ’s daags daaraan gevangen was genomen, ten huijse van gem. Eb geweest zijnde toen aan een zijner slaven zonder dien te hebben genoemd, zoude gesegd hebben dat hij Julij op de plaats van den compt. quaad gedaan, en den zoon van de compt. mitsgs. de knegt aldaar, den eerstgem. op ’t lijf en den anderen in den arm en in ’t been gestoken had; met bijvoeging, dat het egter op die niet gemunt was geweest, maar wel op de baas namentlijk Ehlers selve.
html: Dat wanneer den compt. op Vrijdag den 20 der gepasseerde maand April zig aan Cabo bevonden had, den burger Coenraad Eb hem aldaar hadde verhaald, dat den van ’s compts. plaats weggelopenen en vervolgens aan de Caab gevangenen slaaf Julij des avonds voordat denselven ’s daags daaraan gevangen was genomen, ten huijse van gem. Eb geweest zijnde toen aan een zijner slaven zonder dien te hebben genoemd, zoude gesegd hebben dat hij Julij op de plaats van den compt. quaad gedaan, en den zoon van de compt. mitsgs. de knegt aldaar, den eerstgem. op ’t lijf en den anderen in den arm en in ’t been gestoken had; met bijvoeging, dat het egter op die niet gemunt was geweest, maar wel op de baas namentlijk Ehlers selve.

text: Dat ’t den compt. niet wel bewust was of ’t cabinet waarin de sleutels vermist waren geworden, bevorens gesloten was geweest, dat hij na ’t vertrekken zijner huijsvrouw de sleutel van ’t cabinet in zijn sak gehad hebbende, des namiddags <met den slaaf Julij>  ’t cabinet geopend, er iets uitgehaald en onvoorsiens (zo hem voorstond) den sleutel niet weder bij zig genomen had, dat wanneer hij compt. des nagts gem. cabinet had opengevonden, de sleutel nog in ’t slot steekend bevonden had, gelijk het den compt. volkomen bewust was, dat er geene sleutels buijten die in ’t cabinet geborgen waren geweest, aan de muur hebben gehangen, terwijl den compt. eindelijk bij visitatie niet had kunnen ontwaren dat ’t slot van meerm. cabinet geforceert nog daaraan iets ’t minste gebroken was geworden.

text: TRANSLATION

Today, 13 May 1776, there appears before me, Abraham Faure, secretary of Stellenbosch and Drakenstein, in the presence of the witnesses named below, the burgher Johan Hendrik Ehlers, of competent age, who on the requisition of the honourable landdrost Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, declares it to be true:
html: Today, 13 May 1776, there appears before me, Abraham Faure, secretary of Stellenbosch and Drakenstein, in the presence of the witnesses named below, the burgher Johan Hendrik Ehlers, of competent age, who on the requisition of the honourable landdrost Marthinus Adrianus Bergh, declares it to be true:

text: That on Friday the 20th of the past month April, when the testifier was at the Cape, the burgher Coenraad Eb told him there that when the slave Julij – who had run away from the testifier’s farm and was afterwards taken prisoner at the Cape – was at the house of the said Eb on the evening of the day before he was taken prisoner, he had told one of his slaves, whom he did not name, that he, Julij, had done something bad on the farm of the testifier and that he had stabbed the son of the testifier as well as the knecht there, the first on his body and the other on his arm and leg, while adding that it was, however, not aimed at them but in fact for the baas, namely Ehlers himself.
html: That on Friday the 20th of the past month April, when the testifier was at the Cape, the burgher Coenraad Eb told him there that when the slave Julij – who had run away from the testifier’s farm and was afterwards taken prisoner at the Cape – was at the house of the said Eb on the evening of the day before he was taken prisoner, he had told one of his slaves, whom he did not name, that he, Julij, had done something bad on the farm of the testifier and that he had stabbed the son of the testifier as well as the knecht there, the first on his body and the other on his arm and leg, while adding that it was, however, not aimed at them but in fact for the baas, namely Ehlers himself.

text: That the testifier is not sure whether the cabinet, from which the keys went missing, had previously been locked; that after the departure of his wife, he had the key of the cabinet in his pocket, and during the afternoon opened the cabinet <with the slave Julij>, took something from it and accidentally (as he seems to remember) did not take the key with him again. That when he had found the cabinet open during the night, he found the key still in the lock and, as the testifier was well aware that there were no keys apart from those locked away in the cabinet, he hung it on the wall; while, finally, the testifier did not discover on inspection that the lock of the aforementioned cabinet had been forced open, nor that it had been broken at all.

text: There being nothing further to relate, the testifier asserts to be convinced of the accuracy of his statement as in the text, being willing, if so required, to subsequently confirm the aforegoing with solemn oaths.

text: CJ 2491 Inkoomende Brieven, 1791-1792, Deel 7, ff. 112-114.
Weledele achtbaare heer!

Door de huijsvrouw van den burger Jurgen Radijn is op Zaturdag den 3 deezer mij ter kennisse gebragt dat haaren zoon Barend Radijn den 26 der gepasseerde maand Augustus ’s namiddags zig van huijs naar de plaats van den burger Jan Otto hebbende begeeven, ten eijnde naar haare aldaar wijdende ossen te zien, en des anderen daags terug te keeren, zij, vermits den derden dag geen de minste narigt van ’t agter blijven van haaren zoon had ontvangen, haar daar omtrend geinformeerd, en alstoen berigt bekoomen had dezelve haaren zoon op voorsz. 26 Augustus de Palmiete Rivier gepasseerd en nog op de hoogte aan de andere zijde omtrend een uur deezer zijds de plaats van gemelde Otto gezien te zijn, zonder dat egter haar voorsz. zoon off desselvs paard off iets van zijne equipagie zeedert tot op voorsz. derden deezer, nietteegenstaande alle gedaane nazoek ontdekt off te vinden is geweest, zij dus presumeerde hij om ’t leeven zal zijn gebragt.
html: Door de huijsvrouw van den burger Jurgen Radijn is op Zaturdag den 3 deezer mij ter kennisse gebragt dat haaren zoon Barend Radijn den 26 der gepasseerde maand Augustus ’s namiddags zig van huijs naar de plaats van den burger Jan Otto hebbende begeeven, ten eijnde naar haare aldaar wijdende ossen te zien, en des anderen daags terug te keeren, zij, vermits den derden dag geen de minste narigt van ’t agter blijven van haaren zoon had ontvangen, haar daar omtrend geinformeerd, en alstoen berigt bekoomen had dezelve haaren zoon op voorsz. 26 Augustus de Palmiete Rivier gepasseerd en nog op de hoogte aan de andere zijde omtrend een uur deezer zijds de plaats van gemelde Otto gezien te zijn, zonder dat egter haar voorsz. zoon off desselvs paard off iets van zijne equipagie zeedert tot op voorsz. derden deezer, nietteegenstaande alle gedaane nazoek ontdekt off te vinden is geweest, zij dus presumeerde hij om ’t leeven zal zijn gebragt.

text: Voorts is op voorgisteren avond te agt uuren door zeekere Jan Niemand mij berigt, dat hij neevens een knegt van den manhafften Hendrik Cloete junior, in naame Jan, zonder dat gemelde Nieman [sic] zijn van wist op te geeven en een slaave jonge te paard over de Hottentots Hollands clooff gereeden en aan de andere zijde van de Steenbraazem Rivier gekoomen zijnde, zijlieden buijten den gewoonen weg een Bouganeeschen slave jonge ontwaar waren geworden, en denzelven gevraagd hebbende: Wie hij toebehoorde? had die jonge gezegt: Aan Breda, vervolgens off hij een pas off ander bewijs van zijn lijfheer had? denzelven gezegt had: Neen!

text: Dat zijlieden daarop den bij hun hebbenden jonge te paard op gem. slaaff ingezonden en denzelven toegeroepen hebbende van als dan meede te moeten gaan, gemelde slaaff een mes getrokken en op de voorsz. jonge te paard was ingelopen, die hierdoor terug gedreeven zijnde, en zulx door voormelde slaaff gewaar geworden zijnde, denzelven op een loopen bergwaards had gezet, waarop gemelde knegt zijn snaphaan gelaaden en dien slaaff al vervolgende toegeroepen had van te staan, dog denzelven al voortloopende geantwoord hebbende van zig niet te zullen gevangen geeven en niet willende staan, gem. knegt hem door een schoot met haagel beneeden in de regter dije dermaaten had getroffen dat hij ruijm een quart uur daarna was koomen te sterven, voor zijn dood egter nog gepoogd had, zig zelve met zijn mes om ’t leeven te brengen en alstoen tegelijk beleeden, een slaaff van wijlen de heer Van Cahman te zijn geweest, en door den manhafften Jan Eksteen te zijn gekogt, zig noemende Slammat, en van de plaats van gemelde Eksteen zig na de plaats De Amdandel Rivier te hebben willen begeeven, zonder dat er iets hoegenaamd bij gem. slaaff gevonden is.

text: Weledele achtbaar Heer!
U Weledele agtbaare ootmoedige dienaar!,
[get.] H.L. Bletterman.
Stellenbosch, den 6 September 1791.
TRANSLATION
Honourable Lord!

On Saturday the 3rd of this month the wife of the burgher Jurgen Radijn brought to my attention that her son, Barend Radijn, had set out on the afternoon of the 26th of the past month August from their house to the farm of the burgher Jan Otto in order to attend to her oxen grazing there and to return on the following day. Since by the third day she had not received any notice about the staying away of her son, she had informed herself about it, which is when she got the message that the same son of hers had passed the Palmiet River on the aforesaid 26th of August and was still seen on the height on the other side, about one hour this side of the farm of said Otto, without however her son or his horse or anything of his equipment, in spite of all the searching done, being discovered or found since then up to the aforesaid 3rd of this month; she is therefore presuming that his life must have been taken.
html: On Saturday the 3rd of this month the wife of the burgher Jurgen Radijn brought to my attention that her son, Barend Radijn, had set out on the afternoon of the 26th of the past month August from their house to the farm of the burgher Jan Otto in order to attend to her oxen grazing there and to return on the following day. Since by the third day she had not received any notice about the staying away of her son, she had informed herself about it, which is when she got the message that the same son of hers had passed the Palmiet River on the aforesaid 26th of August and was still seen on the height on the other side, about one hour this side of the farm of said Otto, without however her son or his horse or anything of his equipment, in spite of all the searching done, being discovered or found since then up to the aforesaid 3rd of this month; she is therefore presuming that his life must have been taken.

text: Further, on the day before yesterday, at 8 o’clock at night, I was informed by a certain Jan Niemand that he, as well as the knecht of the manhaften Hendrik Cloete junior, by the name of Jan, without the said Niemand being able to provide his surname, and a slave jongen were riding on horseback across the Hottentots Hollands kloof and having got to the other side to the Steenbras River, they discovered beyond the usual road a Buginese slave jongen and asked the same to whom he belonged; the jongen answered: “To Breda”, next whether he had a pass or some other proof of his master; the same answered: “No!”.
html: Further, on the day before yesterday, at 8 o’clock at night, I was informed by a certain Jan Niemand that he, as well as the knecht of the manhaften Hendrik Cloete junior, by the name of Jan, without the said Niemand being able to provide his surname, and a slave jongen were riding on horseback across the Hottentots Hollands kloof and having got to the other side to the Steenbras River, they discovered beyond the usual road a Buginese slave jongen and asked the same to whom he belonged; the jongen answered: “To Breda”, next whether he had a pass or some other proof of his master; the same answered: “No!”.

text: That upon this they sent the jongen on horseback who was accompanying them after the said slave and having called to the same that he must then go along with them, the said slave pulled a knife and ran towards the aforesaid jongen on horseback, who was driven back by this and when this was noticed by the aforementioned slave, the same started running towards the mountain, whereupon the said knecht loaded his musket and continued to call unto this slave to stand, yet the same, while continuing running, answered that he would not give himself prisoner and would not stand, the said knecht struck him below the right thigh in such a manner with a lead-shot that he came to die within just over a quarter of an hour after it, although before his death he tried to kill himself with his knife and then at once confessed to have been a slave of the late honourable van Cahman and to have been bought by the manhafften Jan Eksteen, calling himself Slammat, and [confessed that he] wanted to have proceeded from the farm of the said Eksteen to the farm De Amandel Rivier, without anything whatsoever having been found on the said slave.
html: That upon this they sent the jongen on horseback who was accompanying them after the said slave and having called to the same that he must then go along with them, the said slave pulled a knife and ran towards the aforesaid jongen on horseback, who was driven back by this and when this was noticed by the aforementioned slave, the same started running towards the mountain, whereupon the said knecht loaded his musket and continued to call unto this slave to stand, yet the same, while continuing running, answered that he would not give himself prisoner and would not stand, the said knecht struck him below the right thigh in such a manner with a lead-shot that he came to die within just over a quarter of an hour after it, although before his death he tried to kill himself with his knife and then at once confessed to have been a slave of the late honourable van Cahman and to have been bought by the manhafften Jan Eksteen, calling himself Slammat, and [confessed that he] wanted to have proceeded from the farm of the said Eksteen to the farm De Amandel Rivier, without anything whatsoever having been found on the said slave.

text: Of all of which finding myself obliged to inform your right honourables with this, who with much respect takes the liberty to call myself,
html: Of all of which finding myself obliged to inform your right honourables with this, who with much respect takes the liberty to call myself,

text: Right honourable lord!
Your right honourable lord’s humble servant!
[signed] H. L. Bletterman.
Stellenbosch, the 6th of September 1791.

heading: CJ 2492 Inkoomende Brieven, 1793-1795, Deelen 8-9 [one volume], ff. 41-44.
text: CJ 2492 Inkoomende Brieven, 1793-1795, Deelen 8-9 [one volume], ff. 41-44.
Wel Edele Achtbaare Heer!

Op ’t aangeeven van den burger Jacob Bieldden 30 Maij jongstleeden in naam en van weegens den meede burger Dirk Gijsbert Verwij, die door ziekte verhindert was zelve bij mij te koomen hoedaanig en op welke wijze zeeker slaaff Zaberlot, die daags bevooren gevangen genoomen was, dien dag is koomen te overlijden, heb ik, geen chirurgijn alhier praesent zijnde, geen zwaarighijd gevonden aan voorm. Verwij te permitteeren voorm. slaaff te moogen doen begraaven, mits egter aan mij, van diegeene welke ’t lijk van voorm. slaaff bezigtigd hebben, ten spoedigsten eene verklaaring onder praesentatie van eede te doen toekoomen, en waaruijt dan volgens zijn opgaaf zou moeten blijken, geen teeken van de geringste mishandeling aan voorm. slaaff te zijn ontdekt ten eijnde aan U Wel Ede. Achtbe. als dan van ’t voorsz. geval kennisse te kunne geeven met bijvoeging der voorsz. verklaaring dan naardien den heere fiscaal mij den tweeden deezer geliefde te communiceeren dat drie slaaven van voorm. Verwij bij zijn edele klagten hadden ingebragt dat voorm. Verwij den voorm. slaaff Zaberlot zoodanig zou hebben mishandelt, dat hij daardoor daags na zijn gevangenneeming zou zijn overleeden, heb ik, vermits daags daaraan heemraads- en den volgenden dag krijgsvergaderinge verpligt ben geweest bij te woonen, twee heemraaden nevens den alstoen praesent zijnden oud oppermeester in dienst der E. Compie. Carel Christiaan Nielle gecommitteerd zig ter woonplaats van voorm. text: En hoe zeer ik vertrouw uijt het een en ander te zullen koomen consteeren de door voorm. drie slaaven aangebragte klagten te zijn ongegrond, heb ik egter welgem. heere fiscaal verzogt dat de eevengem. drie slaaven van Verwij zoo lange in ’s heeren gevangenhuijs moogen blijven, totdat de mij nog ontbreekende verklaaringen ingewonnen hebbende, ik in staat zal zijn mij bij vertoog aan U Wel Ede. Achtbe. en den Edelen Acthbaaren Raade van Justitie te kunnen adresseeren en bij welgem. Rade daarop gedisponeert zal zijn.

text: Waarmeede d’ eere heb te zijn
Wel Edele Agtbaare Heer!
U Wel Edele Achtbare ootmoedige dienaar,
[get.] H.L. Bletterman.
Stellenbosch, den 6 Junij 1793.
TRANSLATION
Honourable Lord!

On the 30th of last May, on the notice of the burgher Jacob Bieldden, in the name and on behalf of his fellow burgher Dirk Gijsbert Verwij, who was prevented by illness from coming to me himself, [describing] how and in what fashion a certain slave Zaberlot, who was taken prisoner the day before, came to die on that day, I, there being no surgeon present here, saw no difficulty in giving permission to the aforementioned Verwij to allow him to have the aforementioned slave buried, on condition, though, that he let me have as soon as possible a declaration upon presentation of oaths by those who have inspected the corpse of the aforementioned slave and from which, in accordance with his notice, it must appear that no sign of the least maltreatment could be discovered on the aforementioned slave, in order to inform your honours of the aforesaid incident with addition of the aforesaid declaration. But since it pleased the honourable Fiscal to communicate to me on the 2nd of this month that three slaves of the aforementioned Verwij brought in complaints to his honour that the aforementioned Verwij had maltreated the aforementioned slave Zaberlot in such a way that he came to die of it on the day following his capture, I, because I was obliged to attend a meeting of the Heemraad the next day and one of the militia on the following day, deputised two heemraden as well as the then present former chief surgeon of the honourable Company, Carel Christiaan Nielle, to go to the residence of the aforementioned Verwij and to have the corpse of the said slave Zaberlot exhumed, thereafter to view, examine and inspect it.  As the same delegates on their return on the 4th of this month reported to me that they did not find on the aforesaid corpse the least sign of maltreatment, but did discover that the face of the same was swollen and that it had one tiny, light, fresh wound on the forehead and two similar but older wounds on the back of the head; while the aforementioned Nielle declares that after he had opened these wounds as well as the chest, and after careful examination and inspection, he concluded that none of these wounds could have been fatal, but that an old chest problem, hunger, thirst and cold, besides the aforesaid wounds, would have given cause for the death of the aforementioned slave, which wounds would have been caused, on account of his resistance, by those people who wanted to take the aforementioned slave prisoner, the first time more than a month ago and now during the last time, about which I have already gathered one declaration and will come to gather two others before long.

text: The general mode adopted by the inhabitants of Cape Town for the disposal of their goods, wares & merchandise. If a shopkeeper or indeed our principal merchants find themselves hard run for cash they apply to the Vendue Master   1.The Vendue Master, more properly the Commissary of Vendues, was a civil officer of the Cape government and the only person in the colony allowed to sell by auction which was "a state monopoly." By 1822, the Vendue Master employed four auctioneers, and a "proportionate number of clerks"; see W. W. Bird, State of the Cape of Good Hope in 1822 (Cape Town: Struik reprint of 1823 edition, 1966), pp. 44-45.  1 for a day for his sale which is regularly entered in a book kept at his office. If the occasion is immediate he gets handbills distributed round the town and affixed at the usual places and the clerks or salesmen have notice to make the sale known at all the auctions they are employed at in the intermediate time by which means it becomes [known] throughout the town.

text: On the morning of the auction a boy   2. i.e. slave.  1   is sent round with a brass dish to tinkle at each corner of the streets to give notice to the inhabitants that there will be a vendue at such a house and by way of encouragement he declares the goods will be sold without reserve. This is not always the case but when the necessities of the seller are great, and immediate the goods are exhibited and at half-past-nine business commences.

text: The highest bidder becomes the purchaser. Sometimes there are two bidders and neither of them will advance a sixpence more. On such occasions the auctioneer takes several pieces of money from his pocket and cries even or odd. By this means they instantly decide who is the purchaser. The money is not paid at the time of the auction as in England & other places    3.  In New York, '"A credit of three, four, or six months, is usually given on sales by the piece . . ."' as quoted in Westerfield, "Early History of American Auctions", p. 176.  1nor is any deposit made at the time of sale. If the person is known or has any friend who will stand forward as his security he has the usual credit of two months after which period he must attend at an office established for that purpose and take up his auction bills.

text: Some of the inhabitants meet with great indulgences from the manager of this concern who is a man of the World, loves to eat and drink of the best things a good providence provider for the sons of luxury and extravagance. A well timed present procures you another month's credit perhaps two and some I am assured now let their accounts remain unsettled six months to the great injury of the principal Vendue Master who is allowed by government great privileges in the disposal of this kind of property. When the sale is concluded the Vendue clerk furnishes you with an extract from his Vendue list which is in general very correct the necessary deductions made for the expenses of the auction salaries duties stamps &c.&c.. This upon being presented to the Vendue Master he pays the amount deducting two and a half per cent for ready money and takes upon himself the whole risque of the property sold. Here is the whole proceeding of the seller. But what are the consequences to the buyer?

text: Many persons who attend these auctions have small shops which from having no capital they gradually furnish by these means and sometimes are very fortunate in their endeavours. Several respectable tradesmen in Cape Town of great property have begun by the same means and now have capitals to import their own merchandise to a considerable amount.    4. Elsewhere Hudson modifies this, pointing out that only the English merchants managed to prosper, the Dutch inhabitants remaining the pettiest of shop-keepers, an observation buttressed by other travellers to Cape Town. William M. Freund points out that even the established Cape Dutch entrepreneurs, e.g. D. G. van Reenen, J. F. Kirsten, and W. S. van Ryneveld "all fared poorly under British rule." Idem, "The Cape under the transitional governments, 1795-1814, "in R. Elphick and H. Giliomee (eds.), The Shaping of South African Society, 1652-1820 (Cape Town: Longmans, 1978), p. 215. Hudson was sometimes a solipsistic observer: what happened to him he often ascribed to some unidentified "many." Possibly, this is his form of self-justification. An excellent example of this trait occurs in his essay on "Slaves," when he informs us that generally the slaves at the Cape are well looked after: his own establishment of slaves is the only one cited, see Ray Bert Westerfield, "Early History of American Auctions—A Chapter in Commercial History," Transactions of the Connecticut Academy of Arts and Sciences 23 (May, 1920): 159ff., esp. 193 et seq.; at this stage we cannot say how many of these findings are directly applicable to the Cape, nevertheless there are sufficient points of similarity to stimulate an investigation.  1 Others who are the purchasers come with a determination to buy to enable them to hold an auction in a few days with the very articles they now purchase to raise money to take up their former Vendue bills. To them the scheme is a very ruinous one and which must evidently end in an immediate bankruptcy. They buy dear. They sell at their own sale without reserve. Of course they must lose considerably upon the first purchase thus: with the additional seven & a half per cent which is the usual expense unless you employ an agent and then it amounts to full 10 per cent.

text: This must in a short time swallow up principal and plunge the unwary adventurer in a prison. Frequently there are very good speculations to be made at Vendues. I have myself attended them constantly for eight or nine years and have many times purchased a variety of articles at these places twenty per cent cheaper than their first purchase from the manufacturer at home and though perhaps not in immediate demand a few months has brought a want of them and they have sold at a hundred and sometimes two hundred per cent profit. The wary old auction hunters who have established themselves by a perfect knowledge of the various articles brought to the hammer and who have some capital to begin with will ever be gainers as 'tis with them a never failing maxim to not purchase but when they are sure of advantage.

text: The principal amusement of the ladies of the Cape is attending these auctions    5. James Ewart, a contemporary of Hudson, confirms this: "...the females, if not engaged at home, attend the venduties or public sales, which they are extremely partial to, and where they are as busy trying to overreach each other in small matters as their husbands are in greater ones." Idem, James Ewart's Journal, covering his stay at the Cape of Good Hope (1811-1814) (Cape Town: Struik, 1970), p. 25; also see Bird, State of the Cape," p. 346.  1 and [they] will sit mixed-up among a variety of frowsy smells that would really make an English woman extremely ill for three or four hours listening to the low and not infrequently obscene jokes of the auctioneer whose chief object is to keep his audience in good humour which can only be accomplished by the witty slang of double entendres suited to the capacity of his motley hearers. There is a great deal of trick and knavery in these sales which the government would act wisely to put a stop to. They have attempted it     6. Possibly this is a reference to the Publicatie issued in November, 1805, which prohibited auctioneers from buying articles for themselves by using accomplices in the audience as fake buyers. The legislation, among many restrictions, forbade the auctioneer from directing the attention of the audience to other objects and then suddenly and unexpectedly closing the sale, PB., 6: 275-76. When the British took over the Cape in 1795, one of their first acts was to confirm the office of Vendue Master; they also streamlined the tax structure somewhat; see PB., 5: 15. According to George McCall theal, this 1795 legislation was "a popular proclamation." Idem, History of South Africa, 1:3.  1 but unfortunately have acted upon a plan started by some person who has mistaken the whole business and instead of remedying has only given a sanction to a system of corruption and left the errors of the whole where they found them.

text: One method too frequently practiced by the sellers is to have several of their friends that they fee by little presents at times to keep them steady in their services who run up their goods to a high price considerably more than their value and this is knocked down to them. The credulous and unwary seeing these old rocks whose judgment they know is infallible become purchasers bid and from one to another the mania spreads and by this trick a tradesman has disposed of his property to a very considerable advantage. another defraud upon government is constantly practiced. all purchases at public auctions above 100 rixdollars are obliged to be upon a stamp of a certain value which rises according to the amount of the sum purchased at one morning or afternoon's sale. Now to avoid this: the wary buyer bids up to 99 rixdollars in his own name but the moment he finds he has upon his list to that amount the purchases in the name of his Wife his sisters Brothers and in short goes around the whole of his connections of relations & acquaintance[s].

text: By this paultry means sometimes saves to himself 20 or 30 rixdollars in a day which is actually defrauding the government revenue of a very considerable sum annually and which might be easily prevented by permitting no person to purchase for others. another scheme is practiced but that carries with it its own punishment. `Tis not unusual for a man to become in the name of a second person the procurer of a great part of his own property. By this means he saves money at the rate of 30 per cent which may sometimes save his sinking credit by enabling him to make a good purchase by which he is assured he can make fifty to 60 per cent but this seldom happens and where it is not the case such exorbitant interest will only hurry him on to that rock he is perhaps striving to avoid. Upon the whole auctions are fraught with good and evil.

text: Half the paper currency in circulation passes through the hands of the auctioneer    10. Hudson might well be correct. Bird calculated that in 1822, there was 3,000,000 Rixdollars in circulation, State of the Cape, p. 35; elsewhere he tells us that "The gross amount of vendue sales" is "computed to be about 250,00 Rixdollars monthly," Ibid, p. 45. During one year then, 3,000,000 Rixdollars would pass through the Vendue Office. The amount of money passing through the Vendue Office during one year was equivalent to all the money in circulation.  1 who is allowed by government 2 1/2 per cent for advancing ready money upon sales. Though this very money is what he has received as the proceeds from other sales which sometimes remain in his hands for a considerable time and draws out in small sums as the convenience of the owner may require it. Therefore he is making an amazing property by the interest of other peoples money. `Tis upon an average about 15 per cent per Year he receives for what money he advances. This I believe is considerably more than our pawn brokers are allowed even adding to the lawful the unlawful practices they make use of. A great deal more might be said respecting Vendues and their good and evil tendency. These few remarks are the result of actual observation in a long residence at Cape Town.    11. If we believe Hudson's title to this set of Essays, the "long residence" could only have been 10 years; however, there is later, internal evidence which suggests that he returned to these manuscripts after 1806.  1 Auctions in the country are conducted in the same manner except it is considered a treat to which people flock for many miles round the country and according to the respectability of the person at whose house the auction is held an entertainment is provided if the company is very numerous.   12. Bird augments Hudson's description: "An auction in the country is an important event for the vicinage. It furnishes what is there extremely rare, a cheerful pastime. A wedding and an auction are the only occasions of lively assemblage. The resort of boers, with their families, from the neighbourhood, is general; from distant places frequent. The ladies repair to the vendutie, dressed as for a gay assembly. The men resort to it as they would to a fair or a country wake. "Idem, State of the Cape, p. 346, and also see pp. 347-8.  1

text: They eat from a clean cabbage leaf instead of a plate & each provides himself with a knife and fork for the occasion as these are seldom furnished by the proprietor of the auction    13. Possibly this was done for the good reason that the cutlery was on sale: James Ewart, however, suggests the cabbage leaf was not a universal phenomenon at rural auctions "Soon after dinner the auctioneer, who was by this time as drunk as his neighbours, commenced selling off the remaining articles which consisted of little more than the wretched utensils in which the dinner had been cooked and served up. . . Idem, James Ewart's Journal, p. 83.  1. Sometimes these sales continue a week and those who come from a considerable distance remain the whole time generally providing themselves with a bed in their wagon which is their usual accommodation when traveling from the interior to the Cape Town. These sales frequently occur as the Dutch Wills generally - if the surviving parties are young - provide for the children in this way.    14. In the Cape colony a form of compulsory partible inheritance prevailed; in contrast to the same practice in colonial America, partible inheritance did not result in sub-division of the property itself. This practice ensured that the heirs in the Cape colony sold the 'family farm' and divided up the money. In colonial Andover, Massachusetts; land itself was divided up until there were many small holdings. These differences in inheritance customs gave rise to quite different settler persistence rates and geographical mobility patterns in the two areas; see Phillip Greven, Four Generations: Population, Land and Family in Colonial Andover, Massachusetts (Ithaca: Cornell University Press, 1970), pp. 83, 130, 230; and R. Cole Haris and Leonard Guelke, "Land and Society in Early Canada and South Africa," Journal of Historical Geography 3 (1977): 135-53. Entail, which has now entered Afrikaner culture, was probably introduced by the 1820 settlers.  1 In case the surviving husband or Wife marries again the property is immediately sold by the Orphan Chamber    15. See p. (000) for a full description; many rural inhabitants took advantage of Vendues organized by the Orphan Chamber by bringing their own goods to such a sale, see `Interdictie' 17th April, 1780, PB., 3: 106. Some colonies in the New World also devised such safeguards for orphans. In Virginia, for instance, where mortality was quite high, at least in the first half of the 17th century, the father often took precautions that his children, and not his widow's husband, would obtain their legacy. E. S. Morgan informs us that; "In making a will, men often named a guardian other than the mother to protect the child's interests, and in addition, appointed feoffes in trust to see that the guardian did his job properly. Where a child was left without either parent, the county court appointed a guardian." Idem, American Slavery, American Freedom: The Ordeal of Colonial Virginia (New York: W . W. Norton, 1975) p. 168.  1 the widow taking one half & a child's share.
